item.title: How the World Gets Its Color Back
item.description:
Attention

How the World Gets Its Color Back

Recovering astonishment through the practice of discernment.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Mental shorthand makes the world manageable, then quietly begins to feel complete.
  • Perceptual training reveals information that was available all along.
  • With practice, discernment becomes less effortful and restores particularity to ordinary experience.
  • Our capacity for astonishment grows as we stop treating ourselves as the center of the world.

“Life shrinks or expands in proportion to one’s courage.” —Anaïs Nin

Our world is an embarrassment of riches. Access unevenly distributed.

A bee sees patterns on a flower that we can’t see. A bird senses the Earth’s magnetic field. An elephant feels vibrations through the ground. A dog can follow a street’s history by smell.

This is the world we share. We say, “That’s amazing,” and move on.

Sometimes we only meet astonishment when David Attenborough lowers his voice. Then the documentary ends, and the ordinary filters return.

Our biology leaves whole dimensions beyond our reach. We can’t borrow a bee’s vision or a dog’s nose. But the boundaries of human perception may be less fixed than our habits suggest.

We associate echolocation with bats. Humans can learn it too. In a 2021 study, blind and sighted adults spent ten weeks navigating their surroundings by making clicks and listening for returning echoes. Both groups improved. Three months later, all 12 blind participants reported greater independence and well-being. The capacity to locate through echo was there all along.

We’ve been selling ourselves short.

What else reaches us but goes unnoticed? Our senses help us handle what’s immediately in front of us. We recognize a face, notice a threat, find the door, read the sign, and keep moving. These shortcuts protect us, but they also let us categorize and move on before we’ve taken in much of what is there.

Over time, what helps us get through the day can start to feel like the whole world. When life becomes just a chain of tasks and reactions, our experience of being alive begins to shrink. The difference may be between meeting the world as it arrives and living inside our meager assumptions about it.

From Difficult to Beautiful

The goal is to perceive more and then read what we perceive accurately. Discernment is perceptual literacy.

Earlier in this series, I used a progression often attributed to Stanislavski: “Make the difficult habitual, the habitual easy, and the easy beautiful.” Most people stop at easy. Here I follow it to the end. What would it mean for discernment to become beautiful?

At first, closer attention takes work: we look again, listen carefully, and question our first reading. But no one wants to stand guard over every perception. Permanent self-monitoring would be exhausting.

With practice, we can develop a second nature. And beyond that, ease becomes style. We can stay in the moment and notice how we are reading it. We meet the world in higher fidelity. A beautiful groove.

A Word Finds Somewhere to Live

In my acting class, the word transcendence came up, threatening to carry us into purple prose about spiritual epiphanies and miracles. I offered something I had seen on my way there: a five-year-old throwing a ball into the air and trying to catch it.

As I spoke, I stood. The folding chair’s legs scraped back behind me. I raised my hands, head tilted, and waited for the imagined ball to come down. The room zoomed in. An actor knows the absolute silence of a transfixed room. The performance of everyday life lasted perhaps ten seconds. It was all right there.

Children have appeared throughout these essays because they have not yet compressed everything into adult shorthand. A puddle, an ant, or a shadow can still command their whole attention. We don’t have to become children again. Experience can help us recover some of that availability. Discernment gives wonder a practiced eye.

Leroy enraptured with his tennis ball. "Join me!"
Source: photo by Daniel Moser

The memory of that boy still teaches me what attention can recover. Speaking of recovery, my dog Leroy’s tennis ball just rolled under the couch. Again. So now, our ritual requires me to lie prone on the rug and fish it out with a broken tennis racket. By the fifth retrieval, it can feel like one damn thing after another. “Leroy, I’m trying to write.” Then, from the floor, I notice his whole body waiting. He trusts me to return the thing he loves.

I swat the ball free. It reappears, and his delight arrives whole, undiminished by the previous four rescues. The love inside his request carries an invitation: Join me.

Now I am trying to recover my train of thought.

Worth it. I’ve got the line:

Sometimes transcendence rolls under the couch.

Learn to Read What Becomes Visible

Seeing more means learning how to read what we notice. Take a coffee mug you’ve used a hundred times. Look again: Where does the light catch the rim? Turn it over. Is there a maker’s mark you’ve never stopped to read?

Find a crack in a wall you’ve walked past all your life. It was there the whole time. The point is to see that the reading can change. Make the familiar strange, then make the strange familiar.

When the World Goes Gray

In the first essay, I asked why important distinctions, including true and false, careful and careless, credible and merely persuasive, had begun to flatten. Here I’m asking what that does to our experience of being alive. Art becomes content. People become types. News becomes noise.

The world goes gray. Not dramatic. Just fading luster.

We are usually not attuned to anything else. We are on stage, performing the lead and waiting for our scene partner to stop talking so we can say our next line. Everyone else, the dog, the bird, the person across the table, is supporting cast. We assume they’re lucky we showed up.

Then something particular breaks through. This child, waiting under this ball. A single bird guided by Earth’s magnetism. Quietly amazing. Color returns when one thing is only itself, and we stay with it long enough to feel that.

What Discernment Costs

On the flip side, seeing more also means seeing what hurts. Unfairness, grief, and fear are harder to file away. Pain can show us where harm is happening, what we have lost, and what matters enough to protect.

It’s easier to stay open when we have time and feel safe. Not everyone does. For some people, reading a face, a room, or a street is how they stay alive. That discernment may begin as survival and carry a real cost. We should not ask anyone to lower a guard they still need.

Even sorrow can return us to what matters. Indifference cannot.

Staying open to what we see takes courage. No one can live in constant rapture. A little more color is enough. The coffee mug is still a coffee mug. We can notice its warmth and get on with the day. We do not have to make every action an epiphany to see the practical beauty of being alive.

Practice discernment long enough, and the world may begin to give itself back in color.

Clicking, buzzing, flying north, waiting for a tennis ball. This is our ensemble.

item.title: Why Therapists Should Be Concerned about AI
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Why Therapists Should Be Concerned about AI

AI is robbing people of purpose. This will soon be a core topic for therapists.

Posted September 30, 2026

Many therapists are concerned about the possibility that they will be replaced, someday, by artificial intelligence. People now ask questions of AI – about mood, about relationships, about life projects – that they might have once asked their therapists instead. And this makes therapists understandably anxious about their professional future.

Source: Pexels/Mizuno K

Will AI Displace Clients Before Therapists?

This is a real concern, but I suspect that it tends to obscure a much more widespread concern: that clients themselves will find themselves, in one way or another, displaced by AI, and that they will be bringing these concerns to their human therapists. The human element of therapy is I believe crucial, and it may be that therapists may ironically be among the last workers to be displaced by AI, and the real problem that they will face will be ministering to their displaced clients.

My office is located within walking distance of two large research universities, and I have the privilege of being able to work with a broad range of talented scientists and scholars. Lately I am noticing an unusual emotion show up in my discussions with these people: despair.

This seems to be the direct result of advances in AI, especially the large language models (LLMs) developed by companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic. LLMs have recently begun solving, within months, problems that have been out of reach of professional mathematicians for decades. They seem poised to make advances in other core sciences as well.

Understandably, this is a source of despair. The despair is not, or not merely, financial. Most of my clients will keep their jobs, or are capable of finding new jobs if they don't. It rather goes to a question of purpose. Being able to make useful contributions to real problems is what gets many people up in the morning. When there is no need for this, because the contributions are made far more quickly and efficiently by AI, then such people tend to experience a crisis of purpose. (This 2025 post by the philosopher Harvey Lederman is a useful meditation on this crisis).

These clients are, admittedly, not typical. But I suspect what I am seeing among these clients is merely the first stirring of a trend that will eventually affect clients and their therapists everywhere. A few years ago, the prospect that a client would be seriously despairing over the rise of AI would seem fanciful, or very rare, unless perhaps she was a professional chess player. Now it is quite real, and growing. I suspect that over the next few years, and certainly over the next few decades, therapists will be seeing this more and more.

This will be a new challenge for therapy. Sigmund Freud famously held that the fundamentals of human well-being are "love and work." Even now, therapists regularly see meaningful work as a measure of flourishing, and unemployment as a "risk factor" for poor outcomes. This work-centered perspective seems ill-suited to a near future when much of our traditional work, especially cognitively-demanding work, will be done, in one way or another, by machines.

How are therapists to prepare for this future, if it is indeed what the future will look like?

One place to begin is a distinction between goals and values, where goals are particular ends we aim at, and values are the principles that guide us in, among other things, our selection of goals. It seems plausible that some of our clients' medium-term goals, at least, will be usurped by machines. If someone's goal is to prove a particular math theorem, then it will likely be usurped soon. If it is to write a fantastic screenplay, then this may take a bit longer, but it arguably will not be very long either. So goals, at least certain kinds of professional goals, will arguably no longer be as central to clients' self-conceptions as they have traditionally been.


Remaining Human Goals and Values Amid AI Progress

This leaves, of course, other goals, such as the goals that clients hold for their relationships and families. It does not appear likely that these will be better achieved by AI, at least not anytime soon. And it leaves, of course, values, such as our pursuit of knowledge or of beauty. The particular ways that individual clients have found to achieve these goals, especially if they work in cognitively-demanding professions or arts, will likely be significantly altered in the near future by the advent of AI. But this simply means that they will need to find new ways of pursuing the values that matter to them, and that clients will need their therapists to help them do this.

This general pattern – the ways in which changes in the world require individuals to make changes in their professional work and self-conceptions – is not new. What is new, if anything, is the rapidity with which it seems to be happening, and the broad scope of people to whom it may happen.

More than anything, I want to suggest that therapists are seeing the AI problem the wrong way around. The problem is not that therapists will be displaced by AI, at least not anytime soon – therapy is a distinctively relational and human profession. The problem is rather that many of our clients may soon find their professional ambitions displaced by AI, and therapists are uniquely positioned to help them through this crisis. For better or worse, AI seems likely to generate plenty of new work for therapists.

item.title: How Is an Emotionally Abusive Family Created?
item.description:
Emotional Abuse

How Is an Emotionally Abusive Family Created?

All it takes is for one parent to emotionally abuse the other.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • A chain reaction is activated when a child witnesses abuse and passes it on to a younger or weaker sibling.
  • An abused parent often takes their anger and pain out on their children by being extremely critical.
  • The abused parent may become so overwhelmed and depressed that they can no longer take care of their children.
  • Other causes of an EAF include parents who are drug or alcohol dependent or who have a personality disorder.

All it takes for an emotionally abusive family to be created is for one parent to emotionally abuse the other, or for one parent to emotionally abuse one of the children. Emotional abuse spreads throughout the family like an infectious disease. The constant criticism, belittling, unreasonable expectations, gaslighting, intimidation, dismissing, competition, and silent treatment get passed on from one family member to the next. For example, if the mother in the family is being emotionally abused by the father, the mother may take the anger she is feeling toward her husband out on her children by yelling at them, being overly critical of them, or by making unreasonable demands. Or, so overwhelmed and weakened by the onslaught of unreasonable expectations, constant criticism and accusations, as well as gaslighting, the abused parent may take refuge in alcohol, drugs, or sleep and abandon their responsibilities and their children in the process, creating another form of abuse—neglect.

In an emotionally abusive family, every member of the family is affected—everyone becomes part of an extremely toxic environment. Absolutely no one escapes the damage. Even the youngest child knows when one or both parents are being disrespectful, critical, or demeaning toward each other.

Research has shown that witnessing emotional abuse is as damaging as actually experiencing abuse. A chain reaction is activated when one or more children witness the emotional abuse of one of their parents and, out of anger or frustration, then pass it on to a younger or weaker sibling. In addition, instead of siblings banding together to offer one another comfort and protection, in an emotionally abusive family, siblings often view one another as either competitors or as enemies.

How Emotional Abuse Spreads Throughout the Family

Emotional abuse spreads like wildfire in a family, having an especially detrimental effect on the children. This occurs because:

  1. Emotionally abusive people generally do not confine their abuse to their partner and often abuse their children as well. Even though an abusive parent may refrain from abusing younger children, many end up abusing them as they get older.
  2. Many recipients of abuse end up passing the abuse along to their children by taking their anger and frustration out on them.
  3. Children also suffer when an abused parent becomes so distressed and/or depressed that they cannot take care of their children properly. Children are left to fend for themselves or to take on the role of having to take care of their parent, becoming what is referred to as a “parentified” child.
  4. Emotionally abused partners often look to their children for comfort and support, often crossing boundaries and creating a situation known as “emotional incest."
  5. In an emotionally abusive family, everyone tends to become either an abuser or a victim. When children witness one parent abusing another on a consistent basis, they will tend to identify with either the abuser or the victim in the situation. Some (often females, but not necessarily) identify with the victim, become a family target, and continue to behave like a victim when they become adults. Others not only take the side of and identify with the abuser, but become abusive themselves.

In addition to the overall damage caused by growing up in a typical emotionally abusive family, there is also the damage caused by special circumstances such as the following:

1. At least one sibling has emotionally, physically, or sexually abused another.

2. One or both parents suffer from a personality disorder or a mental illness.

3. One or both parents suffer from a substance dependence problem (alcohol, drugs).

4. The parents believe in and teach emotionally abusive beliefs to their children.

While all the above information accurately describes the various ways an emotionally abusive family is created, the primary cause at the root of most emotionally abusive families is the fact that one or both parents are likely repeating what they themselves experienced growing up. In other words, parents tend to become like their own parents, repeating the same types of emotionally abusive behaviors, including abusive forms of discipline. In other words, if your parents were emotionally abused by their parents, they will likely repeat the same behavior with you.

In addition, parents tend to reenact the trauma they themselves experienced growing up. As I wrote about extensively in Put Your Past in the Past, what is known as the repetition compulsion propels individuals to repeat the past in an unconscious need to resolve childhood trauma such as emotional abuse.

One of the ways of discovering whether your parents were repeating the way they were treated growing up is to think about how their own parents treat them today. Asking them about their childhood can offer some important information, but many parents have consciously or unconsciously blocked out their memories from childhood, especially if they were painful. Others prefer to take on an unrealistically positive view of their childhood in order to avoid facing the truth. Sites such as ancestry.com and 23andMe.com can provide you with important information about your family history.

I suggest you spend some time remembering what it was like in your home when you were growing up and then write about how your family functioned then and now. This will be a good starting point for your healing, as well as potentially offering a deeper understanding of your family dynamics.

item.title: Old Dogs and New Tricks, a Beginner’s Mind for Older People
item.description:
Education

Old Dogs and New Tricks, a Beginner’s Mind for Older People

Personal Perspective: The challenges of being a beginner when you get older.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • It’s one thing to glorify beginner’s mind and lifelong learning, and another to begin something later in life.
  • If your sense of identity is wrapped up in feeling capable and competent, it’s harder to risk incompetence.
  • In learning new skills as you age, the comfort zone can be a cage and the attitude of expertise an obstacle.
  • When tackling new skills later in life, look for classes geared to adult learners and career changers.
Source: Pixabay/Regenwolke0

I recently went sailing for the first time, a 10-day island-hopping journey through the Gulf Islands in British Columbia. I was with half a dozen friends, but we were also crew, and for most of us it was a crash course in operating a 42-foot sailboat.

One morning, I found myself in an outboard dinghy with two of my crewmates, attempting what’s called a stern tie, where you run a line from the back of an anchored boat to some secure object on shore, and back to the stern.

I’ll spare you the agonizing details, but our operation resembled nothing so much as a Keystone Cops episode, a slapstick display of incompetence, misdirection, and tangled ropes. I ended up chewing on this little fiasco for the rest of that day—or it chewed on me—prompting one of my comrades to ask why it bugged me so much. I told her I felt frustrated at my ineptitude and embarrassed at my poor performance.

I think of myself as a quick learner, agile and coordinated, and possessing ambidexterity and good spatial intelligence. But I felt like a complete klutz at the helm of that dinghy, with my non-dominant hand on the tiller, my dominant hand on the gearshift, my brain doing flip-flops trying to coordinate the two—and all of it exacerbated by an audience.

It’s one thing to glorify beginner’s mind and lifelong learning, to hail the tackling of new skills and the willingness to step outside the comfort zone; it’s another to actually put yourself in the position of being a rank beginner at something long after the beginner stage of life, and especially after a lifetime of cultivating a sense of competence if not mastery in things.

The ability to learn doesn’t have a statute of limitations, or an expiration date, but apparently neither do the mechanisms of embarrassment, humiliation, impatience, and the aversion to incompetence, especially if your sense of identity is wrapped up in feeling capable in the world. The more competent, the harder it will likely be to risk incompetence, whether the skill is sailing, singing, writing, or learning a new language.

In this regard, the comfort zone can be a cage, the attitude of expertise can be an obstacle, and the contrast between being competent and being a rookie can be jarring. As much as I value beginner’s mind, when I was fumbling around in the back of that dinghy, I wasn’t pleased with plowing new neural pathways in my brain. I was frustrated by my high standards getting snagged on my clumsy execution, which was surely exacerbated by belonging to an impatient culture with a skewed view of mastery. A 22-year-old graduates with an MFA and we call that person a Master of Fine Arts. But no one is a master of anything at 22. A master is someone who can take on an apprentice.

It wasn’t always this way, of course. Early in life, beginner’s mind is all there is, and learning is the name of the game: how to walk and talk, read and write, play sports, learn an instrument, socialize and build relationships, become independent, make a living, build a career, raise a family, and more. Fumbling and stumbling are to be expected, and a mentor of mine once told me that if I’m not failing regularly, I’m living so far below my potential that I’m failing anyway.

At some point, however, all this begins to plateau, and we’re coasting contentedly—the pleasures of a tidy, predictable life. (When was the last time you learned a new skill?) The famous comfort zone turns into a dozing familiarity and a calcifying amnesia, each day a ditto of the one before it, making time seem to rocket by in a blur of habit and routine.

At least until the inward urge for novelty and adventure—for aliveness—reasserts itself. Or you’re hit with a wake-up call that forces you back into the learning curve. “Heroes aren’t born,” Redd Foxx once said. “They’re cornered.”

Either way, you have to push yourself out the door, or be pushed. But part of what you’re pushing against in sustaining beginner’s mind as you get older isn’t just laziness and a force of habit, but a few mental and physiological factors that warrant a tip of the hat. The speed at which your brain processes new information and your body tackles physical challenges (and heals from them) gradually slows over time.

This is one good reason, when tackling new skills later in life, to look for classes or communities geared to adult learners, career changers, or people who are “rusty.” When everyone’s in the same boat, learning and failing are easier to bear.

Old dogs, however, can most assuredly learn new tricks. Among dog trainers, it's utter nonsense that you can’t teach old dogs new tricks. Most of them are eager to be physically and mentally stimulated, as long as it doesn’t involve backflips. What’s called “shrinking world syndrome” isn’t just a function of incapacity, but assumptions about aging, whether in our dogs or in ourselves.

Renewal and regeneration are among the calls of getting older, and there’s precedent for it in each of our lives. That is, you’ve been here before, at the place of dreaming your life, needing and wanting to experiment with it, try new things, take risks, find out who you are. It was called adolescence, and some researchers even call the last third of life the second adolescence. Only this one doesn’t come with an entire institutionalized structure designed to encourage the passage from adolescence to adulthood—an educational system. There’s no degree program in maturity. You’re on your own and have to design your own curriculum. And when you become bored with it, redesign it.

I did just that in mid-career—quitting employment for self-employment, which demanded the tackling of a host of new skills and mindsets—and one of the first things I did as a freelancer was to put up on the wall in my new office an old daguerreotype map of the world during what was called the Age of Discovery, the 15th and 16th centuries. At the edges of these old maps, ancient cartographers signified terra incognita by drawing dragons, monsters, ogres, and ships being pulled under by the tentacles of giant squid. It was enough to keep most people safely in the village.

I put that map up there to remind myself that I wasn’t a coward for being afraid of the unknown, and that the willingness to set foot into it is essential to the discovery of new worlds—and the lifelong quest for aliveness. As the French writer Stendhal puts it, “He who trembles is not bored.”

In author Parker Palmer's 2015 commencement speech to the graduating class at Naropa University—whose median age is mid-30s—he said this: “Clinging to what you already know, and what you already do well, is the path to an unlived life. Cultivate beginner's mind, and walk straight into your not-knowing.”

item.title: When Eloquence Prevents Treatment
item.description:
Psychiatry

When Eloquence Prevents Treatment

Anosognosia preserves the power to persuade, which clinicians read as insight.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Anosognosia compromises self-awareness in many people with schizophrenia and bipolar I disorder.
  • My fluency won me a discharge home in 2016, and sent me to jail untreated in 2024.
  • When clinicians confuse eloquence for insight, those who might correct them are rarely asked.
Source: Kari Alfonso/Pexels

A decade ago, at the age of 32, I wanted nothing more for Christmas than to move back into my mother’s house. The times were neither merry nor bright: in the course of nine weeks, I had attempted suicide four times with fistfuls of the psychotropic medications prescribed to me to alleviate my unrelenting anxiety and depression.

A few weeks prior, my mother had pleaded with my attending psychiatrist, Dr. R., not to release me after my most recent attempt had landed me in a medically induced coma in the ICU. She was not wrong to plead. But more than anything, I feared the specter of a third inpatient stay on a psychiatric ward in four months.

And so I built a case for myself, marshalling evidence that made living at home sound like a viable treatment plan rather than the escape hatch that it was. I argued that the IV penicillin had done its work to treat the neurosyphilis that had inflamed my brain—an infection discovered while I was intubated in that ICU. I expressed my terror over the prospect of being forced to participate in the soulless group therapy of a locked ward, or to eat its cardboard food on dining-hall trays next to complete strangers. I assured everyone that I would secure a competent therapist and psychiatrist, as if the process were timely and guaranteed to produce results.

Let me recover at home, I insisted, under the guidance, and with the comfort, of my mother’s love. Against her better judgment, the argument worked, and my mother relented. Dr. R.’s closing admonition to my mother would forever haunt her: “He will be your responsibility.”

A year later, in the midst of an episode of erratic and grandiose behavior, my mother told me that I struck her as manic. She encouraged me to seek psychiatric care, which I took as the utmost of insults. “I am manic,” I shot back, “and you’re going to have to accept it!” The irony was profound: I confidently endorsed the word “manic” while grasping nothing of what it asked of me, a lesson in the limits of merely naming an illness.

I then quarreled with clinicians when they offered a diagnosis of bipolar disorder. Drawing on my years of graduate training, I invoked Michel Foucault when I claimed that psychiatric labels were little more than societal shackles to control any mind, like mine, that dared to speak truth to power. I wasn’t sick; I was transgressive and brilliant.

Foucault’s Madness and Civilization became my intellectual shield against the weapons of psychiatry. I was drawn to how he saw madness as socially constructed, depicting the asylum as a tool of bourgeois order and the psychiatric diagnosis as a technology of exclusion. I saw how psychiatry’s history—what Foucault called a “monologue of reason about madness”—could be easily read as the exercise of institutional power over people designated as deviants.

Seduced by this subversive theory, I camouflaged my illness in it. In a future manic episode, I would refer to myself ostentatiously as the “second coming of Foucault.” What I didn’t understand was how my refusal to accept treatment was an eloquence generated by the illness itself.

Years later, in the wake of my arrest during a period of manic psychosis, I was evaluated by a social worker M. to determine if I would be involuntarily committed before being booked in jail. My behavior was capricious but logically coherent. I flattered her within thirty seconds of her arrival, complimenting her excessively throughout her assessment. I performed a charade of crying before boasting, “See, I can control myself.” I then outlined to her the causes and contours of a severe manic episode—the threats I made against former colleagues and family—while fully in one. But I could not see that I was in one.

And, apparently, neither could she. Although my Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale was positive in all five categories, M. concluded that my behavior was “volitional”—a product of my personality—even as her own note listed possible bipolar disorder and neurosyphilis. And so I was sent to jail and denied psychiatric treatment for another four months.

A few months later, I found myself in a transport van between jails with a man named Sunrise. “Hey, man, could you turn off your brain? I can read your brain waves and they’re bothering me,” he shouted. While his psychosis was overt, mine was disguised and carried an annotated bibliography.

Source: Kaleb Nimz/Unsplash

Sitting across from him, I grasped for the first time what united us: we both lived inside a funhouse of cognitive mirrors of our own making. The difference was that his walls were transparent to everyone while mine were adorned with the artifacts of scholarship and critical theory. As anthropologist Tanya Luhrmann frames psychiatry's dilemma, the patient is either “a rational person with a sickness” or “an irrational person whose irrationality is the sickness.” The honest answer was that I was both but I could see neither.

My blindness was an effect of my decade-long affliction of anosognosia—the neurological impairment of self-awareness that renders many people living with psychosis or mania incapable of perceiving their sickness. Unlike denial, a psychological defense mechanism, anosognosia is the result of a neurological malfunction, striking to varying degrees 50–98% of people with schizophrenia and 35–63% of people with bipolar I disorder.

In an earlier article, I described this as a severance of epistemic authority, the capacity to know one's own mind, from moral authority, the right to make decisions about it. The very machinery of cognitive sight is lost. But while blind, a person under the spell of anosognosia still can speak quite convincingly. All too often clinicians confuse the clarity of that voice for a patient’s insight into their own troubled mind.

Across all these episodes runs the same tragedy of the eloquent refusal: when a mind that cannot see its own illness speaks well for itself, the room too often goes quiet—and the people who know better are nowhere to be found.

Note: This article is the first of three that will outline the intersection of anosognosia and autonomy in the experience and treatment of psychiatric suffering. Here you see the problem from inside the experience of one patient, and next week I will turn to the exclusion of families from patients’ charts, before a final article on potential solutions including discharge planning, capacity assessments, collateral history, and psychiatric advance directives.

item.title: Lessons From a Code Blue
item.description:
Aging

Lessons From a Code Blue

The conversation that matters should happen long before a code blue is called.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Modern medicine can keep a body alive long after meaningful recovery is possible, sacrificing quality of life.
  • Fewer than one in four adults who suffers from a cardiac arrest in the hospital survive to go home.
  • Families making end-of-life decisions without knowing a loved one's wishes carry lasting guilt and doubt.
  • Sharing your end of life wishes ahead of time is a gift that often brings your loved ones peace of mind.

You never really forget a code blue.

When you hear it called overhead on the hospital speakers, your stomach drops because it is every doctor's worst nightmare. It means a patient has stopped breathing or has gone into cardiac arrest. In that moment, every available resource races to the bedside in an effort to save a person's life.

As a new doctor, what I felt was fear. Although we had all been taught what to do, I wasn't confident yet.

Now, almost a decade later as an attending, an automatic reflex occurs as the Advanced Cardiac Life Support algorithm starts running through my head even before I reach the room. For those moments, the person in the bed becomes a body we are trying to restart with medications, chest compressions, and electricity to shock the heart back into rhythm. We often place a tube down the throat so a machine can breathe for them. There is no room for feelings in those minutes; we compartmentalize the fear and grief to focus on what needs to be done.

What happens after the code is another story. Medicine has so much to offer these days, so much technology that can keep the body going for a very long time. And yet we often have so little to offer the family when it comes to quality of life or a better future.

Two Patients, Two Stories

Years ago, I cared for a man who had suffered a stroke that left him in a near vegetative state. He could only breathe through a machine via a tube in his throat. Our testing showed he still had some brain activity, but meaningful recovery was very unlikely. His wife couldn't bear to let him go, and for her, choosing to stop treatment carried a deeply religious implication. We stabilized him and sent him to a long-term facility that would keep his body alive indefinitely.

I also remember a young man whose heart suddenly stopped while he was driving. A series of fortunate events got him to the hospital in time, and CPR and a ventilator saved his life. He went on to make a full recovery and was discharged home.

These two patients, with polar opposite outcomes, both show what modern medicine can do. We begin every resuscitation effort hoping for the second, but the statistics tell a different story. Fewer than one in four adults whose hearts stop in the hospital survive to go home, and some who do are left far from the person they once were. CPR, when performed well, often breaks ribs, bruises or punctures the lungs, and in people taking blood thinners can cause serious internal bleeding.

Why We Avoid the Conversation

Understandably, most of us would rather not think about our own death. Avoiding the topic protects us from fear and uncertainty of facing our own mortality, but it doesn't make the decision disappear. It only hands the burden of that decision to someone else.

And that decision is rarely about whether medicine can keep a body alive. The real question is whether the life that follows, after the trauma of CPR and everything that comes with it, would be one the person would want to live.

When a patient cannot make medical decisions for themselves, the responsibility falls on the family, usually the people who love them the most. Research shows that at least one-third of family members who make these decisions experience significant, long-lasting emotional burden, including stress, guilt, and doubt. Many are left wondering whether they made the "right" choices for their loved one.

I think about that wife often. I don't know what her husband would have wanted, and neither did she. I believe that uncertainty became its own complicated grief layered on top of the loss.

The Conversation I Have at Home

So what would I want if something happened to me?

It's not a pretty conversation, but it's one I have with my husband all the time. Because the more I learn and live, the more I see how limited medicine can be. Yes, it can keep a body alive for a long period of time, but is that what we really want?

For me, the answer is clear. What matters most is quality of life, the soul and joy of living, the feeling of sunlight on my skin, grass beneath my feet, laughter with my family, and connection with the people I love. Even grief and sorrow, experienced alongside that joy, are part of what makes a life fully lived.

Your answer may be different from mine, and it may even change through various stages of your life. You might choose every available intervention for as long as possible, try full treatment for a limited period, or decline resuscitation efforts and focus on comfort care. These are all valid choices. What truly matters is that the people you love know how you feel.

That knowledge is a gift. Research shows that when people participate in advance care planning and share their wishes with their families, their loved ones experience less stress, anxiety, and depression after they die. Knowing what someone wanted doesn't erase grief, but it can certainly bring peace of mind knowing we are honoring our loved ones' wishes.

I, as a physician, never really forget a code blue. After all these years, I still feel that familiar drop in my stomach when I hear one called overhead, and I still run to the bedside ready to do everything I can. But I've also learned that the most important conversations often happen long before that moment. They occur at kitchen tables where the people we love tell us what makes their lives worth living. Those conversations don't take away our hope for a miracle. They simply make sure that whatever happens, the person in that bed is still being honored as who they are, even in their last moments on earth.

item.title: Advocate for Yourself When Choosing Aesthetic Treatments
item.description:
Beauty

Advocate for Yourself When Choosing Aesthetic Treatments

Before you change your appearance, what do you hope to change?

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Take time to understand why you want an aesthetic treatment before making a decision.
  • Set realistic expectations about what a treatment can and cannot change.
  • Advocate for yourself by asking questions, checking credentials, and taking your time.
Source: Paulina Riedler / Used With Permission

Aesthetic treatments have become a common part of how people approach their appearance, as they may influence their sense of confidence and well-being. Aesthetic treatments may be associated with improvements in psychological and social well-being, with reductions in appearance-related distress. Whether it be Botox, laser treatments, dermal fillers, cosmetic procedures, and other aesthetic services, consumers should take the time to understand why they want to pursue treatment, what the risks may be, and whether the person providing the treatment is appropriately trained and qualified.

To better understand the psychological and medical considerations, I spoke with Paulina Riedler, RN, a healthcare entrepreneur in aesthetic medicine. Her experience highlights several practical questions and insights consumers can consider.

1. Do Not Skip the Consultation

Oftentimes, when we want to change something about ourselves, we want to see that change happen quickly and seek instant gratification. I am sure you can relate to seeing someone who does not like something about their appearance and immediately wanting to find a solution.

However, this desire for a quick change can lead people to skip the consultation and rush the decision-making process. For instance, in one study, experts indicated that psychological distress, self-criticism, body dysmorphia, and unrealistic expectations were linked to greater dissatisfaction with previous aesthetic treatments. Taking time to discuss goals, expectations, and concerns with a qualified professional can help slow down the decision-making process and support a more informed choice. As Riedler explained, “Aesthetic procedures are real medical treatments. A thorough consultation allows the provider to determine whether a treatment is appropriate and allows the patient to ask questions before making a decision.”

2. Pay Attention to Your Expectations

Before scheduling a procedure, take a moment to think about what you expect the treatment to change. Will it change how you see yourself? Your confidence? Your internal thoughts about your appearance? People may pursue aesthetic treatments for many different reasons, and wanting to look different does not automatically mean that someone has low self-esteem or a mental health concern. The important question is whether you have realistic expectations about what the treatment can change and what it cannot.

According to Riedler, another important question to ask: “What do you hope this change will mean for you?” For example, there is a meaningful difference between saying, “I would like to soften this feature,” and believing, “Once I change this feature, I will finally feel confident, accepted, or good enough.” If you hope that one procedure will fix several things you are unhappy about, it may be worth stepping back and thinking about what you really hope will change before moving forward.

3. Consider What Is Happening Emotionally

Before engaging with an aesthetic treatment, take a moment to reflect on what may be influencing your decision. For instance, are you choosing the treatment because you genuinely want it, or do you feel pressure to look a certain way because of other people, social media, or recent experiences?

It is also important to recognize the difference between being unhappy with a specific feature and becoming consumed by concerns about your appearance. For example, a 2022 meta-analysis involving 14,913 people requesting cosmetic surgery found that approximately 19 percent met criteria for body dysmorphic disorder (BDD).

BDD involves a significant preoccupation with perceived flaws in appearance that causes distress or interferes with daily life. Simply wanting to change something about your appearance does not mean you have BDD or any other mental health condition. Only a licensed mental health professional can assess for and diagnose BDD. However, if concerns about your appearance are taking up significant time, affecting your daily life, or causing substantial distress, it may be worth talking with a mental health professional before moving forward.

How to Advocate for Yourself Before Treatment

If you are considering an aesthetic treatment, allow yourself time and ask questions. Here are some practical ways to advocate for yourself before moving forward:

1. Understand your motivation: Take time to get to know why you want the treatment and whether that reason feels consistent over time. Ensure this is a decision you want to make for yourself. One question you can ask is: “Why do I want this treatment, and would I still want it if no one else knew I was getting it?”

2. Get an appropriate medical consultation: The consultation and treatment must be with a qualified professional. Many individuals may claim to be qualified to provide aesthetic treatments. Therefore, understand credentials, and know what a qualified professional needs for the procedure you are looking for. When you find them, discuss your health history, medications, risks, alternatives, and expected results.

3. Ask about the product being used: Many products are on the market, many of which are not approved for every type of use. For example, for injectable treatments, you should ask what product will be used, where it comes from, and whether it is approved for the intended use. You have the right to know what is being used as part of your treatment.

4. Set realistic expectations: We know that aesthetic treatments can change appearance, but they cannot guarantee greater self-esteem, happiness, or acceptance from others. Therefore, take time to think about what you realistically expect the treatment to change and what it cannot change.

5. Give yourself time: It is important to remember that you do not have to make a medical decision simply because an appointment, promotion, or provider is available today. If you don't feel comfortable or feel you need more time, it is okay to wait, ask more questions, or get a second opinion.

Bottom Line

In all, seeking aesthetic treatment is a personal decision. Take time to understand the “why” behind your decision, explore your expectations, and consider what is happening emotionally. Taking these steps can help you make a decision that feels right for you and supports your overall well-being.

item.title: If You Want to Declutter Your Mind, Start With Your Home
item.description:
Stress

If You Want to Declutter Your Mind, Start With Your Home

Decreasing our “stuff” correlates with increased mental-emotional well-being.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Physical clutter in our home and work environments actually has a significant impact on our mental health.
  • Research links clutter to increased cortisol levels, stress and anxiety, as well as depression.
  • The question of what items you want to keep is actually the question of how you want to live your life.

When spending time in your home or workspace, how often does it occur to you that there’s just too much “stuff”? What thoughts and emotions does this awareness bring up?

Physical clutter in our home and work environments actually has a significant impact on our mental health. Clutter is linked to stress and anxiety, as well as depression. Research shows that levels of the stress hormone cortisol are higher in people whose home environments are cluttered. Sustained elevated cortisol levels can lead to chronic stress and decreased immune system function, along with anxiety and depression.1

You may believe that you’re unbothered by clutter—defined as a crowded or disorganized mass or collection that impedes movement and/or reduces effectiveness—but its effects can operate beneath the surface of conscious awareness. A study at the Princeton University Neuroscience Institute used fMRI among other approaches to show that the human brain prefers order, and that constant visual reminders of disorganization drain our cognitive resources and reduce our ability to focus. They also found that when participants cleared clutter from their work environment, they were better able to focus and process information, and their productivity increased.2

Other research demonstrates that individuals who feel overwhelmed by the amount of “stuff” in their homes are more likely to procrastinate,3 and a cluttered home environment triggers coping and avoidance strategies like snacking on junk food and watching TV.4

Marie Kondo and Swedish Death Cleaning

Marie Kondo, of decluttering fame, implores people to keep only “what sparks joy.” Similarly, Swedish death cleaning isn’t about clearing out closets. It’s about rethinking our relationship with our things. The question of what you want to keep is actually the question of how you want to live your life. There may well be items that have special significance and evoke genuine meaning. But, upon careful consideration, realistically how many of these are there?

We become mentally and emotionally attached to our belongings because we tend to identify with them—they are representations of who we are or want to be. Unconsciously we tend to relate to our possessions as physical extensions of ourselves. As a result, losing them feels like an amputation of sorts because, in our minds, it is. Now, a degree of such attachment is healthy, but past a certain point, not so much. This dynamic can be obsessive-compulsive and in the extreme manifests in hoarding wherein belongings become so infused with a sense of self that people lose the ability to differentiate between the value of a treasured memento and an old newspaper.

How much we see our things as an extension of ourselves may depend in part on how secure we feel about who we are. Possessions can help defend against feelings of insecurity, and as long as we have our stuff to keep us company we may feel less lonely. Research indicates that materialism—the tendency to seek out possessions for status or approval—is associated with more loneliness and less happiness. But not all possessions are equal. Family keepsakes, and items acquired for their beauty, special utility, or connection with meaningful experiences/relationships don’t show the same correlation.5

Material possessions take up space in our minds, well beyond the available room in our homes. By engaging in an active process of clarifying what’s important enough to hold on to and what isn’t—and letting go of what isn’t—we create more mental-emotional, as well as physical spaciousness.

Strategies for Decluttering

The best time to start is now. As the Tao Te Ching states so profoundly in verse 64, the journey of a thousand miles starts with the very first step. Make decluttering an ongoing process rather than a one-time event. Regularly organizing your home and your workspace, rather than just letting things accumulate, is a beneficial approach to manage mindless accumulation.

Begin with the easy stuff. Clothes are an excellent place to start since many pieces may be redundant or have little sentimental value. In contrast, photographs, personal papers, and family mementos can be the hardest to clear out.

A helpful strategy is to pack things that see little to no regular (or even seasonal) use in a box marked with the contents and the date. After a year, if there’s been no need to open the box, it’s an indication that its contents can be donated or perhaps sold. Between Goodwill, homeless and addiction services, and the proliferation of online communities for buying and selling, there are plenty of options to pass your no longer needed stuff on to others who can use it.

My wife and I now view our accumulation of stuff with a discerning eye toward progressively filling the “give-away box” we keep in the garage. When it’s full, we donate it and then begin again with an empty box.

The bottom line: You are not your stuff—even if it sometimes feels that way. And decluttering our lives is an ongoing journey, not a discrete destination. Rather than one and done, it involves ongoing attention and intention.

item.title: Stop Trying to Get to the 'Next' Thing
item.description:
Wisdom

Stop Trying to Get to the 'Next' Thing

Stop heading to "what's next." The destination is here and now.

Posted September 30, 2026

Source: Chat GPT

Have you ever had a dream that truly offered guidance at just the right time, one that contained an important piece of wisdom you needed to hear? Has a dream ever delivered a message that just felt right, as if it uncovered a truth you already knew on a deeper level—a message that seems to originate from a larger, more mysterious source of wisdom? When this happens, it feels like a gift. Some part of us immediately recognizes the message as true— regardless of whether we like it or not. When this happens, I am always awestruck by the mind’s capacity to weave together exactly the story that will deliver the wisdom we need.

Earlier this year, I was gifted with such a dream, which beautifully and cleverly offered exactly what I and so many of us need to hear. In the dream, I was presented with a logic game. My job and the object of the game was to figure out the right conditions that would allow each of the eight people seated at a dinner table to leave for another destination. The problem was that each of the eight people could move under very specific conditions: Alice, in the first seat, could shift every other Tuesday but only if a man was sitting next to her. Paul couldn’t leave until the guest to his left had gone, while Mark relied on the person directly across the table wearing red. It was a real brain teaser that required Olympic-level mental gymnastics. Each guest had been assigned guidelines for leaving the table, and my job was to derive a seating arrangement and set of conditions for each guest to get somewhere else.

I churned over the instructions, desperately trying to figure out how to make the twists and turns work so the diners could leave the table. Was it on a Thursday in the wintertime, if Perry wore blue and Sheila had just switched with Ken, that all the pieces would fit together? But nothing worked; there was always a block—it seemed unsolvable. I couldn't design a scenario that allowed even a single guest's exit.

And then a profound awareness appeared—out of nowhere. Without knowing why I knew, I realized that the game had been set up to be impossible to solve. I understood with crystal clarity that the answer to the riddle was that the goal I was aiming for was not the goal. The answer was not leaving. The goal was, in fact, for the diners to arrive where they were—to land at the table where they were currently seated. The logic game my dream had constructed in precise detail was like a Japanese Koan, a paradoxical question the rational mind could not solve; it was a task designed to fail. The question was not one that I could mentally muscle my way through to an answer. The resolution could only come with surrender, when all methods of figuring out had dissolved or resolved through insight and realization, or direct sight.

So many of us focus on where we’re headed; we’re on a never-ending mission to get somewhere else, to a better experience, a more pleasurable place—a next destination we presumably can land. Even our physical posture mirrors this internal posture of nexting ourselves. We literally and figuratively lean forward as we walk and talk; our head sits slightly in front of our body as if pulling us towards the next destination. Internally, we live with the subtle but powerful intention to get to a better reality, to arrive at another moment, any moment that’s not this moment—not now. Getting somewhere else is the wallpaper of our consciousness.

Unfortunately, when we’re always trying to get to a future experience, a “then” that’s not now, we’re working against the nature of reality and therefore engaging in an utterly futile endeavor. The irrevocable truth is that it can only—ever—be now. “Then” is an imaginary idea that doesn’t exist in reality. It is always now. This is what the knowing in my dream so thoroughly realized and was there to impart. When we arrive at that future “then” we’d imagined, that “then” will have become the new “now,” which, in our paradigm, will make it uninhabitable. The only place we can ever land or be present in is now. That’s it.

When you notice your mind leaning forward, striving for and focusing on what’s next, see if you can stop and drop into where you are now. Ask yourself: What’s it like right here, right now—drop into your body, your senses. What’s it like when you stop leaning forward, and stop the relentless trying to get somewhere else and relax back into what’s here?

This process does not mean denying or rejecting your desire to get somewhere else; it’s natural. Rather than reacting to it—striving toward somewhere else—relax and include that desire in this present moment and what’s here now. That drive to get to the next thing is part of this now—not separate from it.

The invitation the dream offered me and that I am attempting to offer you is that our goal in life, really, needs to shift from getting to somewhere else—to getting to now. Instead of heading toward a better “table” (with our head leading the way), what if you focused on arriving at the table you’re seated at—landing here where your feet are actually planted. This now is already here and will always be the only experience that’s here. Ask yourself: Have you joined it? Our destination, ultimately, is this.

item.title: Revisiting the Impact of People and Place in Healthcare
item.description:
Health

Revisiting the Impact of People and Place in Healthcare

Quality healthcare needs both a well-designed environment and caring staff.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Research shows that the quality of both the social and physical environment matter in healthcare settings.
  • Views of nature from hospital rooms continue to be important to patients' well-being.
  • The physical environment should support the work of caregivers.
  • Every staff member makes a contribution to the recovery of patients.

In late May, 2026, I was hospitalized for unexpected surgery (thankfully with a good outcome). Ironically, the hospital where I was treated is one I had personally researched. It was part of a field study I did with Claudia Andrade in 2013 involving hospitals in the US and Portugal. The research was funded by a grant from the Academy of Architecture for Health Foundation.

Units at Lawrence & Memorial Hospital

For the research, I studied units in the United States: two units in Lawrence & Memorial Hospital in New London, Connecticut, now affiliated with the Yale New Haven Health System. At the time of the research, one unit on the 4th floor was unrenovated; the other was part of a 5.5-million-dollar renovation in 2013, designed by Moser, Pilon, and Nelson Architects (now part of QA+M). This renovated orthopedic unit, called 4.2, was where I recently recovered from surgery.

The “New” Unit Has Worn Well

This “new” unit, now some 13 years old, looks remarkably as it did when I conducted the US research. The artwork, predominantly representational in nature, is the same, as are the various lounge and work spaces for staff. Over the patient's headboard in many rooms is a triptych of a fern, which may engage visitors, although the patient’s view is toward the opposite wall, where the whiteboard and television are. In the original study, the new unit was rated more favorably than the old unit on almost every dimension (e.g., greater satisfaction with the care received and less stress reported).

A Room With a View: The View Still Matters

Some 40+ years ago, Ulrich (1984) wrote a paper titled “View Through a Window May Influence Recovery From Surgery,” published in the prestigious journal Science. As of September 2026, this paper has been cited almost 4,000 times, according to the Scopus database. Using records from patients hospitalized for gallbladder surgery, some with a view of everyday nature and others with a view of a brick wall, Ulrich showed that those with a view to everyday nature had shorter post-operative stays and also took fewer doses of strong pain medication than did those patients whose view was a brick wall.

One of the lessons of my recent stay on Unit 4.2 is the importance of the view, reinforcing Ulrich’s result. Many patients, me included, had a view that included some kind of nature (for me it was a tree-lined streetscape); however, others, on the opposite side of the unit, had a view of a roofscape and machinery. Clearly, all views are not created equal. In the original study, the view was a source of satisfaction when it included at least some nature; and it was a source of dissatisfaction when a roofscape or other building comprised the view. Designers of hospital units should carefully consider the views that will be afforded all patients (and staff) and attempt to provide every patient with a view of at least some natural elements.

It Takes a Village….Observations About the Role of Personnel in Medical Care

It takes a village to raise a child. It also takes a village to heal a patient, both in terms of personnel and instruments. Over the course of my stay on Unit 4.2, I was struck by how many different roles people played in my care, over various shifts during a 24-hour period. Of course, there were the medical practitioners, from the nurse and PCA to the medical team, including my surgeon. But there were also people who cleaned the floors; people who removed medical waste; people who removed soiled linens; and people who brought food. One of these individuals loaned me her phone charger for the duration of my visit. That generosity made a big difference in my stay because I had a way to be "connected" to loved ones. Although their care takes various forms, every staff member has the potential to make a significant difference in the experience of patients.

Both People and Place Matter

A college president I knew liked to say she could “teach on a rock,” which to her meant that the environment in which one taught mattered little, if at all. It was the person, not the place, that counted. As an environmental psychologist, I have spent my career working to demonstrate the numerous ways in which the environment does, in fact, make a significant difference in human well-being. My recent hospital experience showed me that, yes, the environment matters: Those who deliver healthcare need an environment that supports their efforts, and patients who receive that care benefit from an environment that provides such qualities as positive distraction (e.g., views of nature). Yet, when all is said and done, quality healthcare fundamentally depends on the staff who deliver it. I was fortunate to have superior caregivers in my recent hospital stay.

item.title: Do You Feel Depressed by the State of the World?
item.description:
Depression

Do You Feel Depressed by the State of the World?

If you feel overwhelmed by bad news, taking compassionate action will help.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • It's easy to feel overwhelmed by all the bad news we're bombarded with on a daily basis.
  • If it makes you depressed, try taking compassionate action for a cause you care deeply about.
  • This is an antidote to feeling helpless and can make a real difference to those who are suffering.
Source: Roman Kraft/Unsplash

If you're a sensitive person, like me, it's easy to feel overwhelmed by all the suffering and bad news we are bombarded with on a daily basis. Climate change, wars, the existential threat posed by AI... It's just too much. That's why, in 2025, the Reuters Institute’s Digital News Report found that around 40 percent of people globally avoided the news. They felt overwhelmed and powerless to act.1

This is not a post about politics, or whether progressives or conservatives are right or wrong. It seems to me that we all want to live on a thriving, life-sustaining planet. We want our kids and families to be safe and healthy. We want everyone to have a fair chance at success in life. These values are not ideological, they are quintessentially human.

If you care about any or all of these things — and you're in the 60 per cent of people who do engage with the news — it's easy to feel discouraged, as if everything is bad and getting worse. And, of course, that's what the filter of all forms of news is intended to make you think, because fear, worry, outrage and anger keep us all clicking, scrolling and reading. "If it bleeds it leads," as the old saying goes about what makes the front page.

Stone-Age Brains in a Digital World

One reason we feel so overwhelmed is that our brains and nervous systems are not designed for this modern, hi-tech, digital world. For the vast majority of human history, we lived in small bands of hunter-gatherers, around 100-150 people, out in the wilderness — no smartphones, TVs, internet, newspapers, or radios. Everything we knew, for the entirety of our lives, was about that small group of people, and perhaps the neighbouring tribes. And that's what our brains are adapted by evolution to process.

Now, we are deluged by information from every corner of the globe. If there's a deadly train crash in some remote corner of Pakistan, say, I will know about it in minutes, through social and mainstream media. And because I am a highly sensitive and empathic person, that story hurts my heart. As I scroll through my favourite newspaper's website, I am assaulted by headlines telling me about a whole host of scary, threatening, or upsetting stories. Sometimes I am able to ignore them, but often one story in particular will cut through and leave me frozen; paralysed with an empathy overload at the suffering of some poor child or animal I will never meet.

It's Not Compassion Fatigue

A phrase we hear often is that people have "compassion fatigue", but this is not quite right. What this actually means is "empathy fatigue," because although empathy is a wonderful thing, we can have too much of it. When we read about a famine or natural disaster in our newspaper, see videos on social media, or watch a news story on TV, feeling empathy means putting ourselves in the shoes of those who are suffering and, to some extent, feeling their pain.

There's a lovely saying in Buddhism that to feel empathy means letting your heart tremble at the suffering of another. When we see stories of people suffering, our heart trembles, as it should. But because there is so much suffering in our world, much of which is completely beyond our control, it's easy to feel too much pain and get burned out — leading to empathy fatigue.

As a trauma therapist, I know that feeling empathy is not enough to help another person. I hear terrible stories all the time, and I can't let myself get overwhelmed or paralysed by all the suffering I encounter every day. I know the key is taking compassionate action. That means feeling empathy is a first step, then doing whatever I can to relieve suffering comes second.

This helps us move from helplessness and overwhelm to the feeling that we are doing something to help, however small. Our heart trembles, which motivates us to take action and try, in whatever way we can, to relieve some of the suffering we witness from across the globe.

Give/Do What You Can

Before writing this, I received a fundraising email from Choose Love, a wonderful charity helping refugees and displaced people all around the world. And I gave what I could afford, which of course won't solve all the problems of those who are suffering globally, but might help one child, one family. Doing that small thing helped me feel a little energised and hopeful, not just crushed and helpless.

So if you are struggling right now, start by doing something small. Spend a few hours volunteering at your local food bank. Check in on that elderly neighbour you know might be lonely or might need some help with their garden. Donate to a cause close to your heart, sign petitions, write to your representatives, march, vote, post on social media — there are so many ways we can all make a small but significant difference in the world.

And remember that taking compassionate action not only helps people or causes you care about, it also helps you. It's a win-win, because it shifts you from feeling powerless and depressed to allowing a little hope into your heart. And just think if all of us — all eight billion humans on this planet — took these small steps toward a kinder, more loving and compassionate world. It would be a tsunami of love and care.

And wouldn't that be a beautiful sight to behold.

item.title: Don’t Take It Personally!
item.description:
Anxiety

Don’t Take It Personally!

Three takes on the hard-to follow advice of not taking it personally.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • There is wisdom in trying not to take things personally.
  • Each way is appropriate in different circumstances.
  • There are different ways of not taking things personally.

The things people do can get under our skin. Whether it’s a verbal slight or an oversight, the way they treat us reflects how they see us and the kind of relationship we have.

It's not personal

In a way, the best advice, if you don’t want to spend your afternoon obsessing, is not to take it personally. After all, it isn’t always personal. Sometimes they are just tired, hangry, or anxious about something else. Maybe they ran out of their meds.

In those cases, how they behave is just a distraction. It doesn’t reflect how they really see you, or what kind of relationship you have. Taking it personally, in cases like these, means getting it wrong; misunderstanding them and the relationship you have with them.

“Don’t take it personally!” is great advice for when it isn’t personal. But sometimes it is! Sometimes the way that someone treats you really does reflect on them, and on your relationship. Encouragement not to take it personally, in such cases, is encouragement to get things wrong—in some cases, to get it obviously wrong.

It is personal, but they don't see it that way

Still, what feels obvious can be a mistake. When Cecilia Bleasdale posted a photo of the dress she planned to wear to her daughter’s wedding in February of 2015, it went viral as people discovered that to half the world it looked like a white and gold dress, while to the other half it looked black and blue. What was obvious to many people, including me, turned out to be not true.

A more helpful way to take the advice not to take things personally, if it simply rings false, is as the advice to try to imagine what things might look like, from the perspective of someone to whom it is equally obvious that it isn’t anything personal. Even if you are right and they are wrong, it can be an important step to recognize that things might look so different to them. And that can help you to get along.

You can make it less personal by stepping back

Sometimes, of course, it’s not worth getting along. Some betrayals are not just personal, but heartbreaking.

In these cases, the advice not to take things personally can mean something different. It can be the right advice not because it isn’t personal, or because they don’t see it that way, but because the right way forward is to lower your expectations of that relationship.

If they aren’t giving you what you expect and need from them in the relationship, the right move might be to expect less and skip the pains of disappointment. Someone else is out there who can give you what you expect, as long as you can follow the first two forms of advice: don't take things personally.

item.title: The Link Between IQ and Zip Code
item.description:
Intelligence

The Link Between IQ and Zip Code

Study shows socioeconomic status determines IQ, brain structure, and function.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Socioeconomic status is the prime factor in IQ, brain structure, and function.
  • Differences in IQ, brain structure, and function are contaminated by failing to consider socioeconomic status.
  • Environment affects many other traits, cognitive abilities, brain anatomy and function.
Source: Dr Daniel Bell, Prof Frank Gaillard et al, Radiopaedia.org. License: CC BY NC ND 3.0

IQ is generally considered relatively stable throughout life. This supports the belief that intelligence is largely determined by genetics. From the time IQ tests were first devised in the 1920s to the present day, differences in IQ among people with different genetic backgrounds are evident. New research does not question these facts but instead shows that people have jumped to the wrong conclusions. IQ and brain structure and function are strongly influenced by environmental experience.

In a new study published in the journal Science, researchers from the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis analyzed data from the three largest datasets of brain structure and function associated with many different cognitive abilities, genetics, and other variables, as well as IQ. This includes the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study, which tracks neurodevelopment of 11,870 adolescents in the United States; the Human Connectome Project, which maps brain circuitry using MRI in youth, adult, and aged populations; and the UK Biobank, holding genetic and brain imaging data for 40,000 adults in the UK.

After sifting through 649 variables, ranging from environment, lifestyle, diet, air pollution, chemicals, drug use, infections, and psychological stress (external factors), and also the individual’s traits and health measures, like BMI, genetics, sleep, disease, and genetics, one factor above all had the greatest influence—the person’s zip code.

Zip code captures a person’s socioeconomic environment. Especially for children, the study shows that high IQ and the child’s brain structure and functions associated with intelligence, and several other cognitive abilities and traits that were studied, reflect socioeconomic privilege.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) can measure Individual differences in a person’s innate brain function. Using this method, a person is placed in an fMRI machine and told to do nothing. This so-called resting-state fMRI reveals how neural activity in the brain’s neural networks flows spontaneously, as opposed to when a person is asked to perform a specific task. Well-established fMRI features are associated with high IQ, and other cognitive abilities, traits, and emotional states. Differences in brain anatomy can be assessed by standard MRI, which gives X-ray-like images of brain structure.

The study found that socioeconomic status was the most influential factor in brain differences measured both by fMRI and MRI. Both the brain’s structure, specifically the thickness of the cerebral cortex, and its resting state function were predominantly determined by socioeconomic status.

If this confound is not taken into consideration, studies aiming to correlate brain structure and function with IQ will be contaminated, and indeed predominantly determined, by the individual’s socioeconomic status. This also means that differences in intelligence and brain structure and function that have been linked to a person’s genetic background (race) actually reflect socioeconomic status.

With this new information, and the widely held view that intelligence is fixed at birth, we must now answer the daunting question of how God placed all the smart people in the same zip code. Alternatively, the belief that intelligence is fixed for life and entirely cast at birth by genetics must be rejected. That alternative view is a much more hopeful and powerful conclusion because we cannot change our genes, but we can change our zip code and the social conditions, economy, schools, and opportunities inside it.
