item.title: Navigating the Affordability Crisis in Your Relationship
item.description:
Motivation

Navigating the Affordability Crisis in Your Relationship

Financial compatibility, communication skills, and healthy financial behaviors.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Economic stress can affect relationship satisfaction, conflict, and decisions about partnerships.
  • Structural financial realities and deeply established financial behaviors may be more difficult to change.
  • Financial stress should be treated as a couple problem—not an individual failure.
  • Separate "dream conversations" from "money-management conversations."
Source: Mikhail Nilov / Pexels

One of the biggest challenges facing middle age and younger Americans is the fact that the economic landscape has shifted beneath our feet. Our relationships are being impacted by the fact that wage growth has not kept up with the costs of housing, childcare, and healthcare amongst other fundamental expenditures. The affordability crisis is also a relationship crisis given the direct impact that financial stress has on not only how we navigate issues of money together but also how we choose our partners.

Understanding Financial Compatibility in Relationships

Let’s start with financial compatibility and expectations. Compatibility can be composed of lifestyle goals (or expectations), financial behaviors, and each individual’s ability to reach those goals independently. According to the Urban Institute, since 2017 home prices have increased by 81% and rent by 54% while wages only grew by 43%. Even though there is some evidence in some pockets of the U.S. that home ownership is growing amongst middle-aged single women, a majority of Americans can’t afford to purchase a home even in a dual-income household. Current mortgage interest rates make that even more difficult.

That’s why a sober understanding of a potential partner’s earning potential and financial behaviors is especially critical during economically challenging times. Healthy relationship skills and communication can be learned but there may be financial constraints around your partner’s profession or career that will remain consistent and unchanged. Likewise, spending and saving behaviors can also be modified but long-standing patterns are more often predictive of alignment in the long-term.

Starting conversations about money with a dating partner of 6-months or longer can be a good way to get a sense of their comfort about such conversations. Anxiety and avoidance, lack of transparency, and defensiveness should concern you. The earlier couples start talking about finances, the better (Saxey et al, 2024). These conversations can start with self-disclosure and can occur over time, not a one time talk. Here are a few examples:

  1. I’m making saving and investing a priority this year. How important is saving or investing to you right now?
  2. I’ve had to whip out my credit card more than I’ve wanted over the past year. What’s your philosophy of using your credit card?
  3. I was looking at my budget recently and it’s been really helpful, do you have a budget? Is that a thing for you?

Effective Communication Strategies for Long-Term Couples

For readers who are already in a long-term relationship, there are two broad communication strategies that will be helpful. The first is related to financial stress and the second is about your dreams/aspirations. There can be a painful psychological contradiction occurring for many relationships where couples may think to themselves that they’re doing everything they can but still can’t afford the lifestyle they expected or wanted. These can turn into identity issues and relational issues:

"Why aren't we further ahead?"

"Why can't you earn more?"

"Why did we buy this house?"

"Why are we still renting?"

"Why can't we have children yet?"

"Why can't we afford to travel?"

It is recommended that financial stress be conceptualized as a couple stressor versus an individual financial management problem or personal failing. Couples should steer clear of criticism and contempt toward their partner or themselves. Validating each other’s concerns and stress is a practical way to avoid these toxic behaviors and help reduce each other’s stress. That can happen in any check-in with your partner but also during a “Stress Reducing Conversation” where you can ask each other about the most stressful part of your day, week, or month, summarize what you’re hearing from your partner and communicating that it makes sense they feel the way they do.

Likewise, it is important to stay connected to each other’s dreams and bigger-picture goals as they often come with financial realities. Carving out time every 6-12 months to check-in with each other’s longer-term goals or the goals of the relationship (i.e. saving for a home, having a child, etc.) is key. Problem solving and action planning is not the goal of these conversations. The goal is to stay connected to each other’s dreams, validate them, and honor them.

Lastly, one of the most important and healthy financial behaviors for a long-term partnership or married couple to engage in is creating a shared budget and scheduling time to explicitly check-in on financial goals. These conversations should be separate from dreams conversations and can be focused on the realities of the period you’re reviewing and/or planning for moving ahead. It’s often the case that one partner is tracking shared expenses and savings. However, it is helpful to have both partners understand how to access shared accounts, produce cash flow or other reports with whatever platform the couples use to manage accounts, and come to these meetings ready to actively collaborate to review and modify the couples’ budget.

Beyond the power of our vote for policy makers who we believe will represent our economic interests the best, we individually don’t have influence over tariffs, wars, housing shortages, and other external factors of this affordability crisis. Yet in our own relationships, we can have a significant impact on how we experience financial stress and mitigate its impact on our relationship satisfaction. It’s up to us to keep getting better at doing that and reach out for couples therapy when we need help.

item.title: Who Cares for the Person Caring for the Pet?
item.description:
Animal Behavior

Who Cares for the Person Caring for the Pet?

Understanding the comfort and challenges of caring for a companion animal.

Posted September 30, 2026

The other day, during an interview, someone asked what topics come up in my clinical work when clients talk about their pets. As I listened to my own answer, I noticed that I was talking about bonds, connection, and the support animals provide. That made me realize that pets also come up in conversations about stress, the challenges of caregiving, grief, of course, as an important aspect, and the difficulty of caring for an animal when you are dealing with a significant mental health issue yourself.

Although we are beginning to discuss the complexity of the bond between people and animals, I think that complexity is still often obscured by a romanticized view of that bond. This view may have an impact on how the bond with companion animals is addressed in daily conversations or in clinical conversations.

Examining the Impact of Companion Animal Bonds on Mental Health

The connection between the field of human–animal interaction and applying this knowledge in clinical settings is still emerging, particularly when it comes to understanding what to ask and how to approach issues related to the bond with companion animals when they arise in therapy. This bond has become increasingly important in people’s lives, so it is not a surprise that more and more people have been interested in understanding how this emotional connection can impact people’s mental health and well-being.

A recent article examined the comfort people receive from their pets and the difficulties they face in caring for them. The study included 210 people living with HIV who had a pet. Although its findings cannot be generalized to other populations, the article made me reflect on how relevant it can be to understand the practical difficulties people encounter when caring for their animals.

In this study, the researchers accounted for factors such as income, housing status, and perceived social support. Although participants reported high levels of comfort from their pets, difficulty affording veterinary care was associated with symptoms of anxiety and depression, even after accounting for these other factors.

Why Clinicians Should Recognize Both the Comfort and Challenges of Pet Care

I see significant clinical relevance here. The article invites us to consider how people experience their bond with a companion animal, including both the comfort that relationship provides and the difficulties of caring for that animal. It also draws attention to the support, or lack of support, available to people in their role as caregivers.

At the same time, from a clinical perspective, I perceive a gap in clinical training when it comes to addressing the relationship clients have with their pets and its possible clinical relevance. Although this gap is not intentional, it may have an impact on clinicians' ability and confidence to meaningfully address these themes in their clinical work.

It is quite common for people to mention their pets, whether in response to questions such as “Who do you live with?” or “Who is part of your family?” or when describing everyday moments in which their animal is present. Clinicians therefore have many opportunities to consider this relationship and explore whether it has clinical relevance by examining its impact on people’s lives. A key challenge here is to translate knowledge from the human–animal interaction field into conversations in therapy.

These reflections have shaped my thinking when writing the book “Conversations about companion animals in clinical settings”, which is an invitation to explore and build that bridge between knowledge that often remains within the human–animal interaction field and its practical application by clinicians working directly with this dimension of people’s lives.

Making Room for Curiosity

We know how essential it is to adopt a curious stance in clinical practice, and perhaps this is precisely what we need to cultivate further, including when people talk about their pets.

For example, some people bring concerns about caring for a pet or coping with their loss into therapy. Being curious about their experience of caregiving is also important, particularly when an animal is ill or receiving palliative care.

In this context, some studies have highlighted the significant stress that can be associated with these responsibilities. Therefore, looking only at the possible fear of losing the pet or the comfort associated with their presence is as important as understanding the possible stress associated with these experiences.

Sometimes I hear statements such as, “On top of that, I have my cats or dogs to take care of.” Not rarely, this kind of perception reveals how caring for an animal may add new layers of complexity to situations that are already demanding.

Recognizing this complexity and questioning idealized assumptions about life with pets matters for research and for clinicians supporting people whose mental health concerns may be directly or indirectly connected to their relationship with a companion animal.

In other words, when someone mentions their companion animals in therapy, they may be telling us about connection and love, but they may also be communicating the effort it takes to take care of themselves and another being. This role can feel even lonelier when overlooked in care-related contexts, such as clinical spaces.

item.title: The Magic of Resilience
item.description:
Resilience

The Magic of Resilience

How to cultivate resilience when you need it.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Resilience is a set of skills you can practice and strengthen.
  • Being resilient doesn’t mean you don’t feel fear, grief, or overwhelm.
  • Regulating your nervous system and taking small steps can help restore flexibility and agency.
  • Noticing tiny joys helps you stay connected to what’s good, even when life is hard.

Picture the worst thing that has happened to you this year. Maybe you got laid off at the worst possible moment (not that there’s ever a "good" moment). Or, perhaps you got dumped by the person you were convinced you were going to spend the rest of your life with. Or, you got a life-changing diagnosis.

What did you do after that thing happened? Maybe you cried, or yelled, or frantically called your sister. But then, you kept going. You went to bed and got up in the morning; you ate something; you got a breakup haircut. You found some way to keep moving, even if it was clumsy and tearful, and you are still desperate to grow out those bangs.

That capacity to get through the worst thing is resilience. And it’s not something you have or don’t have; it’s something you can cultivate, which is the best news I have for you today.

What Is Resilience?

The American Psychological Association defines resilience as “adapting well in the face of adversity, trauma, tragedy, threats, or significant sources of stress.” In other words, it’s the thing that makes you keep on keeping on. As researchers studied resilience, they expected that they would find a fixed trait – something that some people naturally have, and others don’t. As it turns out, that’s not true at all. Resilience is a set of skills and strategies that can be taught, practiced, and strengthened.

Developmental psychologist Ann Masten famously calls resilience “ordinary magic.” It's magic because it can carry us through the unimaginable, but it’s also ordinary because it’s something we all have. As with all things that are ordinary, though, we tend to take it for granted or miss it entirely.

This is partially because we use the word resilience wrong. We assume that “adapting well in the face of adversity” means adapting stoically. We believe that resilient people don’t have emotional responses to the bad things that happen to them. If in the midst of some darkness you’ve had the thought, "I should be handling this better," you’re missing your own ordinary magic.

Resilience in Practice

First of all, let’s get this myth out of the way: You can be resilient and have strong emotional reactions. Fear, anger, grief, and overwhelm are completely appropriate responses to difficult circumstances. They are not signs that your resilience has run out or that you didn't have any to begin with. This belief is something we have layered onto resilience, but it’s not in the original definition. Nowhere does it say that resilience is "the absence of distress." It is the ability to feel through the distress and keep going.

It helps us adapt to distress by ensuring that we have enough space and resources to remain flexible. In an emergency, our attention and our ability to adapt tend to shrink. When the walls close in, flexibility is the first thing to go. So how do we hold onto resilience in the midst of a storm?

Here are three quick tips to cultivate resilience when you need it:

1. Regulate, regulate, regulate: Here’s the thing: When we are dealing with a stressor that isn’t immediately resolvable, our nervous systems can get stuck in the "danger" position. This is why you can feel exhausted but wired at the same time, and it's what leads you to find yourself rehearsing worst-case scenarios at 3 am instead of sleeping. The key here is to make nervous system regulation a daily priority. Think small: a gentle walk, a few deep and slow breaths, or a conversation with someone who never fails to make you laugh.

2. Focus on the smallest possible next step: When we’re in a crisis, we naturally want to solve everything all at once. Say you get laid off. What you really need to do is get your things out of your desk and maybe stop at the grocery store on the way home. But instead, you start spinning out about how you’re going to pay your rent, what jobs are out there that you can apply for, and how to get health insurance. Instead of getting stuck in the overwhelm of those problems, pivot.

Find one concrete, achievable action and complete it. It could be something so small it almost seems silly. Send an email to your old boss. Fill up your water glass. Take a shower. Accomplishing one small thing restores something important: your sense of agency. It reminds your brain and body that you can still do something. You don't always need to know how you'll get through the next year. Sometimes you only need to know what you'll do in the next six minutes.

3. Notice what's good, even when it's tiny: When we're in crisis, we over-focus on what's going wrong. That's a survival technique, and it has served humans well. But it simply doesn't give us an accurate picture of the world. Yes, things are hard, and there are also still good things happening, even if they're small. This isn't toxic positivity because it doesn’t deny the negative things. It’s mental flexibility, the ability to hold more than one truth at once. For example:

  • I have no idea how this is going to work out, and my friend just sent me a voice memo that made me laugh so hard I snorted.
  • Today has been an absolute dumpster fire, and getting into clean sheets tonight is going to feel great.
  • I have a bunch of hard things to do today, and this cup of coffee is giving me life.

That last one is my favorite. The coffee itself doesn’t fix anything, but noticing that it is still here, and that you can still enjoy it even when things are hard, is profoundly restorative.

And remember, resilience is a practice. The goal isn't to become someone who is unaffected by adversity. The goal is to become aware of your own ordinary magic, so you are increasingly able to know your innate capacity to meet difficulty with flexibility.

item.title: What Does It Mean to Flourish?
item.description:
Happiness

What Does It Mean to Flourish?

Humans seek to flourish, but we often look in the wrong places.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Common views of flourishing include pleasure, wealth, and honor.
  • Flourishing depends on cultivating a virtuous moral character.
  • We acquire moral virtues through our intentional actions we do habitually.
  • People who flourish have security and stability within themselves that enable them to weather life’s troubles.

What is the final or highest goal in human living? What is the one thing that, if you have it, there is neither anything you need beyond it nor anything better than it? These questions have occupied philosophers for millennia and keep the rest of us busy as well.

Many people would answer, “happiness,” which leads to asking what counts as happiness. I will follow the lead of Aristotle (384-322 BCE), who argued that many common conceptions of happiness fall short of being the highest good or goal. Nearly 2,400 years later, these views of happiness persist.

Three common concepts of happiness that people tend to offer are pleasure, wealth, and honor or status. Aristotle rejects each of them:

Pleasure: We share all sorts of pleasures with other animals, and human happiness is not just different from, but higher or better than, canine happiness, for example.

Money-making: We don’t want money for its own sake but rather for what it can buy (status, influence, or acceptance as well as material goods).

Honor: We want the approval of others, but that makes our happiness contingent on others. What is honorable this year may be regarded as dishonorable the next.

What is flourishing?

Having cleared the board of possible contenders, Aristotle offers his definition of happiness as “rational activity of the soul in accordance with virtue.” To avoid confusion over the term “happiness,” let’s call this “flourishing.”

Human beings aim to flourish. That is our highest goal, according to Aristotle. To understand human flourishing, we need to have a picture of human nature.

According to Aristotle, our human nature comprises rational capacities, appetites, and emotions. Our reason must have dominion over our emotions so that we can act in appropriate ways that situations require. This is how we cultivate virtues, according to Aristotle.

A virtue is the mean between two extremes of excess and deficiency. Consider the virtue of courage. A cowardly person does not act at all; instead, they may just avert their gaze. A rash person explodes onto a scene and acts without a plan or sense of the possible outcomes. The courageous person deliberates about possibilities and acts even while still feeling some fear.

When we deliberate and choose actions that are appropriate and are done for the right reasons, we acquire virtues and cultivate our moral character. We become who we are by what we do habitually. We become virtuous by doing virtuous acts repeatedly. We can also become vicious people by regularly acting in vicious ways.

To flourish is to cultivate moral virtues through your actions, intentionally design your moral character, and then act from that character. Only morally virtuous people can flourish genuinely, according to Aristotle.

The hypocrite who “passes” as virtuous may be morally vicious even if some of his acts bring about good results. He cannot flourish. The coolly rational person who never does virtuous acts is not flourishing either, according to Aristotle.

A good moral character provides stability and security

To flourish isn’t to feel pleasure and happiness all the time. Rather, flourishing is a way of living that is stable and durable, enabling us to feel the pain and suffering that are just parts of our lives but not lose ourselves to it. And when we flourish, we can also experience great joy and pleasure without losing ourselves to it.

People who flourish will be okay even if they presently cannot imagine what being okay would look like. They know their character, and they know what they are capable of doing and surviving.

For those of us who have struggled with addiction, especially when we are early in recovery, we may feel that trying to change our relationships with alcohol, other drugs, and behaviors such as gambling, scrolling TikTok, eating, and having sex is all burdensome—that these behaviors have taken too much from us and that we’re no longer in control.

Having to change when we do not really want to change becomes even more burdensome—especially when others are pressuring us to do so. We may come to believe we have to change because of those external constraints or consequences such as losing our job, our spouse, or our family. This indeed is a burden to bear, especially when you are the one who has to give up so much. It may seem like a terribly unfair exchange or even extortion.

Over time, many people shift their attitude about the work they do in recovery. Instead of it being a burden and something that they must do, it becomes something they get to do because they are no longer under the influence.

Struggling with addiction and working in recovery give people the opportunity to become more aware and appreciative of who they are and how they are in the world. They have the opportunity to more intentionally compose their character. That is what it means to flourish and to belong to yourself, which provides the stability and security to weather life’s storms and appreciate its calm.

item.title: 3 Reasons Not To Use AI for Relationship Advice
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

3 Reasons Not To Use AI for Relationship Advice

An instant AI answer may soothe your hurt while hiding the full story.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • AI only knows the story you tell it.
  • AI can flood you with possibilities that can drive you to overthink by losing trust in your own instincts.
  • AI can not have a genuine conversation with you.

We all value feeling reassured when we feel hurt. Maybe your partner seems distant, or your adult child just sent you an angry text. Or a friend of yours cancels your plans, once again at short notice. Your brain jumps to what their behavior surely means, and AI can offer a welcome dose of validation in moments like these.

As a psychologist, I am struck by how many of my clients tell me they turn to AI after painful interactions like those above. And I really do get it, because when you are upset, it can feel like a big-time relief to put your thoughts into an AI query and get an immediate response. But a quick, smoothly written, AI response often misses what's going on between two people below the surface, especially when it's based on only one person's perspective. Let's now dig even deeper and look at three further reasons to be cautious when turning to AI for relationship advice.

1. AI Only Knows the Story You Tell

The reality is that you are loading the dice when you roll it skewed with AI as your confidant, and that is a big deal. Suppose you ask, "Why was my partner so hostile when I got home?" This question already implies some interpretation. Maybe your partner had a valid reason to feel angry with you, or perhaps they were worn out from caring for your sick child. In other words, AI can't read your mind (or your partner's) or know what you haven't told it, and you may not even know all the details yourself yet.

Recently I wrote about jumping to conclusions and separating what happens from what we think it means. For instance, "My partner spoke sharply is your observation based on their voice and body language. But "They don't care about me" is an interpretation. The point is that even though your hurt merits attention and you may be tempted to get that met with AI, the interpretation you get back may not be valid.

2. AI Can Flood You With More Possibilities That Drive Your Overthinking

In my book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me, I discuss painful conflicts between parents and their adult children. After receiving an angry message, a parent may reread it repeatedly, searching for a clue about what will happen next. I have written a lot about overthinking, and I often see how seeking reassurance can backfire. In this case, let's say you go to AI for another explanation, hoping it will finally put your mind at ease.

But guess what: now you feel flooded as AI doles out freshly minted interpretations as quickly as you can ask for them. Each answer likely gives you only brief, temporary relief (because you are stuck in a maddening overthinking loop) before you feel compelled to ask again; then you are just feeding that worry loop instead of stopping it.

3. AI Cannot Have A Genuine Conversation With You

Whoa, hold on, you may be saying to yourself, "Dr. Jeff, how out of touch are you? AI sure feels like it can have a conversation with me!" Well, I'll give it to you that AI can suggest what someone's words could mean. Still, it cannot tell you what the person actually intended, listen to their response, or repair a misunderstanding between you (especially given that your relationship's history and context are packed into your brain, not that chatbot's).

Don't get sucked into the illusion that an AI-polished answer feels like progress while the actual conversation you need to have (which may likely be messier) remains undone. How about instead saying something (live, in real life, to the actual other person) like "Our recent exchange hurt me, and I'd like to talk and better understand what happened. I'm committed to a calm, constructive conversation so we can both better understand each other." And then there's the magic part that moves mountains and heals relationships: Listen, really listen without you filling in the blanks or letting your AI "friend" fill them in for you.

Final Thoughts

The urge to get an immediate answer from AI can seem to make sense, especially when we are hurting. Instead of turning to AI, though, slow down and ask yourself: What do I really know, what am I assuming, and what human-to-human conversations or decisions would actually help?

item.title: 7 Strategies People Use To End Draining Friendships
item.description:
Friends

7 Strategies People Use To End Draining Friendships

Ending a stale friendship is a complicated process, but it can benefit you too.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Gradual distancing is the most common strategy for ending draining friendships.
  • People use seven main sub-strategies, from ghosting to frank conversations.
  • Immediate termination is rare and used in situations of serious betrayal.
Source: Liza Summer / Pexels

A new study published in Personality and Individual Differences explores the dynamics of undesired friendships and how they can be far more complex and prolonged than the dissolution of romantic relationships.

According to Psychologist Menelaos Apostolou of the University of Nicosia in Cyprus, Greece, terminating an undesired friendship might be a necessary evil you need to practice for the sake of your happiness and well-being.

“Having a good network of friends is crucial for leading a happy and fulfilling life, a fact that motivated me to research the phenomenon of friendship,” explains Apostolou. “The network of friends people can have is limited, so by terminating friendships with individuals who are not good friends, people release space in their network for individuals who could be good friends.”

While we’re usually mindful and specific about the qualities we desire in a romantic partner, we might be inclined to defer evaluating the quality of our friendships. However, having friendships that do not fulfill us or exhaust us can lead to dissatisfaction and an inevitable breakdown of the bond.

“In general, people want friends who are supportive, have good traits such as humor, are similar to them, provide social input, and are available,” he explains. “People may come to realize that their friends do not satisfy these criteria, which would motivate them to end their friendship with them.”

A friendship enters troubled waters when the amount of resources one member is pitching in is not reciprocated by the other for a prolonged period of time. In such cases, the study posits that “it would pay for individuals to terminate a poor quality friendship, which would enable them to reduce resources that they know would not be reciprocated, and open a slot in their social network, which could be filled in with a friend with desirable qualities.”

Therefore, if there is a friend in your life who never shows up, targets your insecurities, or is unreliable with their finances and depends on you to take care of them, contemplating cutting them off would not be an outrageous reaction. According to the study, it might all be a matter of allocating your resources, emotional and material, keeping your mutual best interest in mind.

Apostolou’s study attempted to identify the techniques people use to terminate friendships through open-ended questionnaires followed by a statistical analysis. The study found that people typically use one of two strategies to dissolve friendships they no longer view as essential to their lives:

  1. Gradual termination involves slowly but surely distancing yourself from an undesirable friendship until the bond eventually fades away.
  2. Immediate termination involves cutting a friend off directly and abruptly, as soon as one realizes that the friendship is not good for them.

These two categories were arrived at after having chunked together seven sub-strategies that emerged from the statistical analysis. These include:

  1. Avoiding spending time with them
  2. Having a conversation
  3. Turning your conversations more formal
  4. Talking to them in an unpleasant manner
  5. Making excuses to avoid them
  6. Gradually fading out
  7. Ghosting

“In general, people seem to prefer to use the gradual termination,” says Apostolou. “One possible reason is that this strategy is less likely to create bad feelings and retaliation that comes from them. Yet, the choice of a strategy would depend on various factors such as one’s personality or the situation. For instance, if your friend sleeps with your girlfriend, you will probably go for the immediate termination strategy.”

For anyone who finds themselves in the murky position of considering ending a friendship, Apostolou has the following advice:

“I would also say that it is not a good idea to rush to terminate a friendship if something goes wrong,” he warns. “Instead, it is better to spend some time assessing a friendship, give second chances, try to place yourself in the other person’s shoes, and consider if you have behaved properly toward your friend.”

Friends who stand by you through your trials and tribulations are invaluable. It may be worth considering, however, if maintaining the friendship itself feels like a burden. You may be better off without the dead weight of a friendship that does nothing but empties your cup, after having made multiple attempts to restore the balance.

item.title: How to Create a Schedule That Allows Spaciousness
item.description:
Mindfulness

How to Create a Schedule That Allows Spaciousness

4 tips for maintaining space in your daily life

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Spacious awareness and flexible thinking promote well-being.
  • Demands on our daily lives and beliefs about productivity can make it difficult to cultivate spaciousness.
  • These suggestions can help you create and maintain room in your life to invite spaciousness.
Source: Liz Roemer / used with permission

Co-Authored By Lizabeth Roemer, Ph.D. and Josh Bartok, M.S.

We wrote over the summer about the ways that expanding your awareness and your thinking can help you thrive amid sociopolitical and personal stress and offered suggestions for practices that can help you cultivate spaciousness. However, one significant barrier to cultivating spaciousness of mind is an absence of space in our schedules.

There are, of course, many demands on our time: more tasks at work than our scheduled workday can fit, child- and other family-care responsibilities, a relentless bombardment of many sources of information that demand our attention, and countless other values-based or necessity-based activities that can easily fill each day. Moreover, many people have to work multiple jobs, take unreliable and slow public transportation or walk, and lack child-care support that others have.

On top of these demands, we often receive societal messages that suggest that being busy is a sign of importance, that doing is more valuable than being, and that one’s worth is capitalistically tied to one’s productivity. These messages can lead us to fill our schedules even more than external demands require, leaving us with very little time to take a step back and reflect on how things are going, take stock of our emotional reactions, consider possibilities, or identify changes we want to make.

This demanding context can leave us feeling like we are barely keeping up with our lives and that we have little agency over how we spend our time. These tips may help.

Refrain from filling every hour of your schedule

For those of you who are lucky enough to have some control over aspects of your schedule (the meetings you schedule at work, the number of tasks you agree to, the additional responsibilities you take on), take the time to be intentional about what you schedule and what you agree to. It is easy to look at your calendar and see any openings as times you are “available.” However, downtime is necessary for uptime.

Some open time in your schedule is necessary for you to thrive in your work, your relationships, and your personal growth. Unscheduled time is not, in fact, “available”—in an important way it’s already spoken for. Try to find ways to protect some open time so that you can breathe, reflect, and make non-reactive choices about your life.

It’s helpful to even go so far as to mark off open times on your calendar to protect them for these important activities. You might choose 15-, 30-, or 60-minute blocks, depending on what works best in your life. And when a meeting or other commitment is canceled or runs short, consider this an opportunity for you to cultivate spaciousness, rather than rushing to fill in that time with additional obligations or tasks.

Schedule regular check-ins with yourself

In addition to scheduling regular open times that allow you to naturally cultivate spaciousness, you can also intentionally check in with yourself to see whether you have enough space in your days (or weeks, or months). Consider putting a check-in time on your calendar every one to three months or so in which you intentionally consider how the rhythm of your life is going, whether you are spending time in ways you would like, and specifically whether you have enough space in which to reflect, consider alternatives, and make choices about how you are spending your time. If not, try to find some small ways to make this time in your current context.

Pause before saying yes

Our aspirational contributions to work, family, and community often exceed our de facto capacity. When considering your true capacity, recognize that it includes your emotional capacity, your energy level, your physical health, and the rest of what may be going on in your life.

So when you receive requests or opportunities, or you develop your own ideas of projects you want to take on, first pause to consider your capacity in your current context—your life as it actually is right now, not as it was last month, or how you wish it were. And when trying to discern how much time a new task might take, rather than imagining what it would be like if everything goes right, imagine things going wrong. Ask what you can give up in order to fit this new responsibility in your life. Consider what you will end up giving up if you don’t make an intentional choice. And then decide from this more fully informed perspective, rather than assenting from the entrenched habit energies of people-pleasing.

Notice and consider what nourishes you and what drains you

We all have obligations and responsibilities that drain us—but we can’t only engage in activities that drain us, because we will eventually diminish our capacity to do anything at all. Pay attention to the activities you engage in that leave you feeling more spacious, more connected, and more energized, and make sure you are making space for those too. They are, in a very real way, also utterly essential.

As you begin to create more space in your daily life, revisit our suggestions for cultivating spacious awareness and spacious thinking.

Josh Bartok is a contemplative photographer and life coach, and the author of two children’s books.

item.title: How We Create Our Relationships in Everyday Communication
item.description:
Relationships

How We Create Our Relationships in Everyday Communication

The ordinary moments with a partner often mean more than the grand gestures.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Relationships are continually made and remade through communication.
  • As we change, we may need something different from our relationships.
  • The strength of our relationships is one of the best predictors of long-term health.

Most of us speak of relationships as things we have. We tend to think of a marriage or a close friendship as something that simply stays the way it is. Relationships, however, are always in the making. We remake them again and again through the ways we communicate with one another, often without realizing we are doing it.

The phrase “speaking of relationships” carries two meanings for me (and is why I chose it as the name of this blog!). The first is simple: this is a place for talking about all things relational, from the families we are born into to the ones we choose, and yes, even that ex. The second comes from years of studying how people communicate to make sense of their lives and relationships.

We often think of communication as sending and receiving messages, as though our relationships exist somewhere apart from the things we say to one another. Scholars have long argued the opposite, that relationships are created in communication and negotiated over time. In this sense, speaking of relationships also means speaking them into being, one interaction at a time.

Relationships Are Revised in Conversation

Even when relationships are hard, every conversation brings another opportunity for revision. We can easily lose sight of this when we feel stuck, whether the same argument keeps resurfacing or a friendship seems to have drifted too far to find its way back. Yet research on recurring arguments shows that partners who see their disagreements as resolvable tend to report stronger relationships. In any relationship, approaching a problem as something we can work through may say more about the relationship than how often we argue or how long hard times last. The conversations that sustain a relationship can also change its course, or bring it to a close. Our past patterns need not decide how things will be.

Of course, it is not only our relationships that change; we do too. Life leads us in directions we expect, and in others we never saw coming. The people we become may need something different from the relationships we began years before. Communication gives us a way to make sense of those shifts together, even when they do not come at the same time for each of us.

Still, communication is not a cure-all, despite the popular advice to “just communicate.” Some issues do not begin with too little conversation and will not end with more of it. Words have at least as much power to wound as they do to heal, and most of us have learned that some things, once said, cannot be unsaid. Recognizing this gives us all the more reason to speak with care.

Relationships Are Essential to Our Well-Being

Grand gestures can seem like the moments that matter most, but our relationships are largely defined in the ordinary. They are built and sustained in moments that seem almost insignificant. According to the longest-running scientific study of adult life, the strength of our relationships is one of the best predictors of our long-term health. The quality of our communication directly influences the quality of the relationships that are critical to living longer, healthier, and happier lives. In other words, the conversations we tend to take for granted are doing some of the most important work for our well-being.

Whether we realize it or not, we are always speaking our relationships into being. We do so in everyday moments, from the inside jokes no one else would understand to the stories we tell and retell over the years. A handful become memories we carry with us long after the conversation ends. All the while, relationships are made in the ordinary conversations that become the history we share.

That is why relationships are so endlessly worth talking about. They are always in the making, and so are we.

item.title: Could Validation Help New Parents?
item.description:
Parenting

Could Validation Help New Parents?

Research highlights a step for tired parents to tend to their relationship.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Couples can really feel the strain of becoming parents, and how partners relate to each other matters.
  • A new study looked at the link between validation and how couples manage the shift to being parents.
  • Partners who validated each other in disagreements also enjoyed a better relationship after becoming parents.
  • It’s possible to learn how to validate a partner.
Source: Helena Lopes / Pexels

If you’re not a parent, you might imagine that parenthood changes just about everything. And if you are a parent, then you certainly don’t need anyone to tell you that. You are all too aware!

When couples step into their role as parents, they can feel the strain of this shift and tend to be less content in their relationship. So what do we do with that knowledge? Say, “Oh well! That’s just how it goes!” and do a proverbial shoulder shrug? I guess we could, but that would be pretty dissatisfying, and it wouldn’t do couples any good. Thankfully, psychologists aren’t doing that.

Research shows that how partners communicate with each other really matters. This is true for couples generally, and for partners who become parents. But what can partners actually do to tend to their relationship?

In a new study, researchers asked couples who were about to become parents for the first time to talk for 15 minutes about issues they disagreed on. The research team also asked couples various questions before parenthood and six months into their lives as parents. In particular, they focused on the relationship between validation and how couples fared as they embarked on their journey as new parents.

You’ve probably heard about validation, but let’s get into the weeds a bit about how to define it and what it involves. When partners validate each other, they’re trying to show they’re paying attention and genuinely appreciate how their partner feels and sees a situation.

Bear in mind that validation is not the same as agreement. People can validate each other while they have different points of view. It’s basically a way of saying, “I recognize that you’re a different person with your own legitimate feelings and ideas, and I can empathize with you and grasp where you’re coming from.” Examples of validation include:

  1. Body language and sounds that show you’re following along (e.g., “ah, mmm-hmm”).
  2. Letting someone know you grasp what they’re saying (e.g., “Right, what you’re saying makes sense. I get that.”).
  3. Paraphrasing, which involves putting what you’re hearing into your own words (e.g., “So, when last night didn’t go how you were hoping it would, you felt really down.”)

The results revealed that validation was linked with eased tensions. When one partner validated the other partner’s upset feelings, the partner who was in distress was more apt to shift out of that distress and into a more comfortable emotional place. The results also showed that partners who validated each other amid their differences were more content together several months into being parents.

It’s not possible to say that validation caused these beneficial conditions. However, as the research team also noted, validation involves specific techniques that people can learn, and it’s worth helping partners learn how to bring them into their relationship.

item.title: 5 Signs that Now is a Good Time to Start Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia
item.description:
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

5 Signs that Now is a Good Time to Start Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia

CBT-I is the gold standard for insomnia disorder. Is it the right fit for you?

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • CBT-I is recommended by medical guidelines as the treatment of choice for insomnia disorder.
  • CBT-I typically lasts for 4-8 sessions and performs as well or better than hypnotic sleep medications.
  • These five signs suggest that CBT-I may be the right choice if you are suffering from insomnia.
Source: Katrin Bolovtsova / pexels

If you have trouble sleeping at night, you are in good company. Up to one in ten adults in the United States struggle with insomnia disorder at any given point in time.

Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) is recommended by the American Academy of Sleep Medicine as the treatment of choice for insomnia disorder. CBT-I is a brief, therapeutic intervention that takes 4-8 sessions on average. Research suggests that CBT-I works as well as or better than hypnotic medications for improving sleep quality and quantity, with fewer side effects. Individuals who complete CBT-I also tend to continue to see additional improvements in sleep even after the treatment ends.

While completing CBT-I, you will keep a sleep diary, which allows your provider to make personalized recommendations based on your unique sleep-wake patterns. During the treatment, you will also learn techniques such as stimulus control, relaxation, and cognitive flexibility to improve your sleep. CBT-I involves much more than just sleep hygiene and can be life-changing for people who have long been suffering from poor sleep.

If CBT-I is the first-line recommendation for insomnia, does that mean it will work for you? Although there are never any guarantees when starting a new type of psychotherapy, here are five signs that now could be the right time to start CBT-I:

  1. You consistently have trouble sleeping. If you have difficulty falling or staying asleep as frequently as three nights a week over a period of three months or more, you may fit the diagnostic criteria for insomnia disorder. Other important criteria include significant emotional distress or impairment in your daytime functioning, and the sleep problem existing despite having plenty of opportunity to sleep. This latter distinction is important - if you are up all night taking care of a new baby, for example, you may not meet the criteria for insomnia because you don’t have sufficient opportunity to sleep. If you regularly still cannot sleep after the baby drifts off, however, then CBT-I might be a good fit.

  2. You spend a significant amount of time lying awake in bed. Some folks struggle with lying awake at the beginning of the night, spending hours just willing themselves to fall asleep. Others fall asleep with few issues, but wake up for long stretches throughout the night, unable to drift back to sleep. Still others wake up too early in the morning - well before the alarm goes off - and are involuntarily awake for the rest of the day. CBT-I is extremely effective at reducing the amount of time you spend tossing and turning, which can allow your bed to finally feel like a cozy, calming environment again.
  3. You are frequently tired during the day. Some people are genetically short sleepers - meaning that they actually need less sleep than the average person to be physically and mentally restored. This subset of folks may consistently sleep surprisingly little at night, yet never feel fatigued or distressed during the day. For the majority of us, however, sleeping less than 5 or 6 hours each night would lead to daytime sleepiness. If you fall into this latter camp, CBT-I might be a good fit for you.
  4. You have tried many other solutions. Folks with chronic insomnia have often tried a myriad of strategies (and sometimes spent a small fortune) in pursuit of ever-elusive sleep. The list of attempted solutions can be endless: mattresses, cooling devices, blue-light glasses, a slew of medications, supplements, even surgeries. It can be difficult to think about attempting one more strategy. Thankfully, CBT-I has the research to back it up as an effective way to improve sleep.
  5. You are willing to make a significant change in your sleep behaviors. A lot of people think CBT-I involves the types of tweaks that might be included in sleep hygiene recommendations, which is not accurate. You may be asked to make significant changes to your sleep, including the timing of when you get in bed and how long you stay there. Because of the biological factors that impact sleep, such as circadian rhythms and daily sleep load, you need to be ready to stick to these changes for several weeks in order to see the full benefit.

item.title: Do We Still Have Agency When AI Helps Us Decide?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Do We Still Have Agency When AI Helps Us Decide?

With AI, we are more productive but have less agency in our lives.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • AI can influence which possibilities we consider before we realize there’s a decision to make.
  • Having the final say doesn’t guarantee we’ve questioned whose purposes a decision serves.
  • How we use AI today may change our capacity to decide for ourselves over time.

Imagine receiving an email that rubs you the wrong way. You start to type your reply, then realize how irritated you are. You feel the heat rising and your fists clenching, but you don't want anger in your message, so you turn to your favorite AI companion for help. Of course, the response is excellent—better than anything you could've imagined. It's much calmer, and it makes your position clear, so you make a few minor edits and hit send.

But did AI really help you accomplish what you wanted? A quick, convenient response might make it harder to find out. Your AI assistant certainly helped you with the framing and wording, but how much agency did you actually have in creating your response?

Many of us wonder whether AI will eventually wake up and develop human-like autonomous agency—and then use it to kill us all to fulfill its mandate to make more paper clips. After all, humans are drawn to imagining apocalyptic futures. But a more urgent question might relate to what’s happening to us right now. We seem to spend an inordinate amount of time focusing on the doomsday scenario and paying far less attention to whether our increasing reliance on AI systems will fundamentally alter the kind of agency human beings can exercise.

Are we moving from being the authors of our own lives to becoming functional biological executors of algorithmically curated choices? Is it possible that we’re retaining physical actions but surrendering the authorship of our lives?

I define agency as the capacity to see more than one possibility, choose intentionally, and believe our choice matters. Recognizing when we’re angry and asking for help can be an expression of agency. The question is how much say we have in what happens next. AI can help us see options we hadn't considered before and work out how to act on them, but we might also start treating those options as the only ones worth considering or trust its recommendation more than our own judgment. Sending an AI-generated response means we’re still making a choice; however, did AI help clarify what we wanted the conversation to accomplish, or did we accept its approach because the wording sounded right?

In that email exchange, agency means seeing that a suspiciously well-drafted reply is only one of many ways to respond. Other alternatives might include asking why the person drafted their note the way they did before defending our position, picking up the phone and calling them, pausing for a few moments (or days) before responding, or talking to somebody else to process our emotions. Intentionality means considering what we want the human part of our interaction to accomplish, and whether that aligns with our beliefs and values. And believing our choice matters means recognizing that we have the capacity to act and that how we respond can affect what happens, even if we can't control the other person's reaction. An AI-drafted reply might get us past a difficult moment quickly without helping us understand what we truly wanted from the conversation or what we can learn from the experience.

In a recent study, participants were asked to write about whether social media was good for society. Those assisted by AI received suggestions generated by an assistant deliberately designed to favor one side. Some found themselves heeding those suggestions before deciding what they actually wanted to say, and they often applied minor word edits while keeping the AI’s underlying framing. What’s even more interesting is that they still felt in control because they could change the text, even when the assistant had helped determine what they were arguing.

This study doesn’t establish that AI is causing a lasting loss of our agency, but it gives us reason to pause and question whether just approving a suggestion means we've thought through what we want it to achieve. My concern is what might happen if we become accustomed to the direction supplied, especially when the results are often so good that we rarely feel a need to reconsider.

Before asking AI to draft that difficult email, explain what you are unsure about in the relationship, or better yet, talk it through with someone (maybe a human) who might offer a different perspective. You may discover that what you wanted AI to help you with was sidelining an emotion that might be giving you important information; your reaction became a convincing email that landed in someone else’s inbox, and you found yourself defending a position you were never sure you wanted to take in the first place.

The conditions around us matter too. In her new book, Situated, psychologist Angela Duckworth argues that we often underestimate how much our surroundings influence our thoughts and actions. Instead of relying on raw willpower in a difficult environment, exercising agency means changing your surroundings to support your goals. AI becomes part of those surroundings when we bring it into a decision. Asking it to draft a reply immediately creates different conditions for thinking and acting than asking it to help us examine why the email upset us or waiting until we’ve decided how we want to engage with the situation before bringing it into the process. We have some say in those conditions.

Go back to your email draft. You might still want to send exactly what AI is proposing after having worked out why it’s the response you want to give. My concern is what happens when the draft sounds so good that we send it before asking ourselves what we want from the conversation. We’ve dealt with the email, but we may still be unsure what to do about whatever made it difficult to answer. If using AI gradually changes how we practice our agency, could we become quicker at replying but less able to work out what we actually want to say?

item.title: Integrating Behavioral Health and Medicine Makes Care Whole
item.description:
Integrative Medicine

Integrating Behavioral Health and Medicine Makes Care Whole

Behavioral healthcare is healthcare. Let’s build systems that reflect that.

Posted September 30, 2026

Key points
  • Behavioral healthcare continues to be treated as a lower priority in our healthcare system.
  • When behavioral health needs are not addressed, patients may feel unsupported, delaying their recovery.
  • If behavioral healthcare is truly healthcare, our systems should better align and reflect that belief.
  • Behavioral healthcare should be available as readily, reliably, and routinely as other forms of healthcare.

As we approach World Mental Health Day on October 10, we will again hear a familiar statement: “There is no health without mental health.” You will find very few people who disagree. However, the way healthcare is organized sends a very different message.

Even though mental health holds a much more prominent role in our national dialogue, behavioral healthcare continues to be treated as a lower priority in our healthcare system. It is still commonly financed, delivered, and discussed as though it exists somewhere just outside of the healthcare system. Patients needing mental health services are sent to different providers, through different referral systems, utilizing different insurance networks, with limited coverage and reimbursement rates. Behavioral health records often remain separate from medical records, and communication between mental health professionals and medical providers is frequently inconsistent or nonexistent.

So, although we are fond of saying behavioral health is healthcare, our systems very often do not behave in ways that validate the statement.

The Problem With the Model

Our current model assumes medical care addresses the illness first and foremost, and behavioral healthcare can address related consequences later.

If a patient has trouble recovering from a heart attack, managing diabetes, adjusting to cancer treatment, or coping with chronic pain, only then does mental health enter the conversation, and consideration is given to whether depression, anxiety, trauma, substance use, or family stress might be contributing to the health challenges. Unfortunately, this approach treats behavioral healthcare as an afterthought. The physician treats the “illness,” and only later is a behavioral health professional called in to address any complications.

This model seldom serves either patients or physicians optimally. When behavioral health needs are not addressed, patients may feel unsupported, and their recovery may be delayed. Physicians may see symptoms continue unabated while their otherwise sound treatment plan falls short with no logical explanation.

We must move to a model in which behavioral health care is not just reserved for when “noncompliance” with a medical treatment plan becomes an issue or when the plan fails to produce the desired results. Human behavior and experience are embedded within every healthcare encounter, every treatment plan, and every outcome. Patients must recognize their symptoms, seek care, communicate with their clinicians, take prescribed medications, deal with side effects, alter daily routines, and sustain behavior change over time. Very often, they do all this while frightened, in pain, and juggling financial, family, and occupational pressures. None of these factors are peripheral to healthcare. Instead, they meaningfully affect whether patients can benefit from it.

More Than Treating Mental Illness

In order to do that, it is important to dispel the myth that behavioral healthcare only treats psychiatric disorders. Psychologists and related behavioral health professionals help people improve sleep, manage chronic pain, develop better health behaviors, cope with the aftereffects of serious diagnoses, support family members experiencing caregiver burnout, and make complex treatment plans and decisions work within the realities of their daily lives. The work of behavioral health professionals addresses how patients experience illness, how they participate in treatment, and how they maintain their health. This work is critical, putting behavioral health squarely within healthcare rather than at its margins.

Separate Systems Create Barriers

Take a moment to consider what happens when a primary care provider identifies depression and recommends therapy for a patient. A typical mental health referral usually starts with the patient having to confirm insurance coverage for the service and what it entails, then going through a list of phone numbers to locate a provider that falls under that coverage, secure an appointment, arrange transportation, and start from scratch explaining the situation that led to the referral in the first place. The burden falls entirely on the strained patient or guardian, adding to the problem instead of helping solve it. Without integrated systems, the primary care provider may never know if the care was received, while the behavioral health professional may have little or no access to the medical treatment plan.

Integrated Systems Promote Health

If behavioral healthcare is truly healthcare, our systems should better align and reflect that belief. Behavioral health professionals should be included and involved more meaningfully before concerns become crises. They should be involved before patients are labeled difficult, unmotivated, or noncompliant. Mental health screenings should lead to meaningful care in the moment and not just another referral list. Coverage, reimbursement, information sharing, and professional education should facilitate collaboration among psychologists, physicians, nurses, pharmacists, and the broader healthcare team.

World Mental Health Day gives us an annual opportunity to help increase awareness and reduce stigma surrounding mental health, which also means integrating behavioral health into the care team and bringing down the systemic barriers that make accessing care too heavy a burden. A true measure of our commitment to better mental health is whether behavioral healthcare is available as readily, reliably, and routinely as other forms of healthcare.

Our patients do not experience their mental and physical health as separate parts of themselves, nor should we ask them to navigate a healthcare system that does.

Behavioral healthcare is healthcare. Let’s commit to building systems that reflect that.
